topics.topic: Development of practical skills in biology

questions.prompt:
(i) Give three common errors students make when plotting a graph of absorbance against ethanol concentration. (3)
(ii) Explain how carrying out replicates improves the investigation. (2)
questions.solution:
(i) Axes not labelled / missing units [B1]
Non-linear / uneven scale, or scale using less than half the grid [B1]
Points joined dot-to-dot with a smoothed curve / extrapolated beyond the data / plotted inaccurately [B1]
(ii) Allow anomalies to be identified and excluded [B1]
Means can be calculated, increasing confidence / repeatability [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain when a line of best fit should be straight, curved or replaced by joining points with straight lines. (5)
questions.solution:
Straight line of best fit when the relationship is linear [B1]
Smooth curve when the relationship is clearly non-linear [B1]
Join points with ruled straight lines when intermediate values can't be predicted [B1]
Line should pass close to most points, with roughly equal numbers above and below [B1]
Don't force through the origin unless justified [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how to use a colorimeter correctly. (5)
questions.solution:
Choose a filter of complementary colour to the solution [B1]
Zero the colorimeter with a blank (e.g. distilled water) [B1]
Use the same cuvette, wiped clean, inserted the same way round [B1]
Fill cuvettes to the same level; avoid bubbles / fingerprints [B1]
Use a calibration curve of known concentrations to convert absorbance to concentration [B1]

questions.prompt:
Two students compared their maximum oxygen uptake (VO₂max) after 30 minutes' exercise. Student 1 concluded that his higher value was because he was heavier.

Give three variables that were not controlled. (3)
questions.solution:
Fitness / amount of training [B1]
Age / sex / height / body composition [B1]
Type or intensity of exercise / time of day / food eaten / health / smoking [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why investigations involving people are hard to control, and how scientists reduce this problem. (3)
questions.solution:
People vary genetically and in lifestyle, so many variables can't be controlled [B1]
Use large samples, so individual differences average out [B1]
Match groups (age, sex, fitness) / use the same person as their own control / randomise [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why VO₂max is often given in cm³ kg⁻¹ min⁻¹ rather than cm³ min⁻¹. (3)
questions.solution:
Larger people use more oxygen simply because they have more tissue [B1]
Dividing by mass allows fair comparison between people of different sizes [B1]
Shows how efficiently the body supplies oxygen per unit mass [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how you would plot data showing the rate of stem elongation (mm day⁻¹) at five concentrations of gibberellin. (4)
questions.solution:
Concentration (independent variable) on the x-axis; rate (dependent) on the y-axis [B1]
Both axes labelled with units [B1]
Linear scales using more than half the grid [B1]
Points plotted accurately as crosses, joined with straight lines or a line of best fit [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain when you should draw a line graph, a bar chart and a histogram. (4)
questions.solution:
Line graph when both variables are continuous [B1]
Bar chart when the independent variable is categoric / discrete [B1]
Histogram for frequency of continuous data in classes [B1]
Bars in a bar chart don't touch; histogram bars touch [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how error bars (e.g. ± 1 standard deviation) on a graph help you interpret results. (4)
questions.solution:
Error bars show the spread / variability of repeat readings around the mean [B1]
Large error bars show low precision / reliability [B1]
If error bars overlap, the difference may not be significant [B1]
If they don't overlap, the difference is likely to be real (confirm with a statistical test) [B1]

questions.prompt:
The number of urine samples testing positive for testosterone was 180 in 1988 and 66 in 1991.

Calculate the percentage change. (3)

In one year, 4.2 % of 3500 samples tested positive. The next year 2.8 % of 5000 tested positive.

Calculate the number of positive samples each year and comment. (3)
questions.solution:
Year 1: 0.042 × 3500 = 147 [M1]
Year 2: 0.028 × 5000 = 140 [M1]
Percentage fell, but the number of positives barely changed because more samples were tested [A1]

questions.prompt: Calculate the mean annual decrease if positives fell from 240 in 2010 to 96 in 2016. (3)
questions.solution:
Decrease = 144 [M1]
Years = 6 [M1]
24 per year [A1]

questions.prompt:
The number of positive tests for steroids fell between 1988 and 1991. An official claimed this showed that steroid abuse was being reduced.

Evaluate this claim. (6)
questions.solution:
Data support the claim — positives decreased [B1]
But we need to know the total number of samples tested, so percentages can be compared [B1]
Athletes may stop using steroids before tests / use masking agents [B1]
New steroids may not be detectable by existing tests [B1]
Fluctuations in other years — trend not consistent [B1]
Only testosterone tested; correlation does not prove the cause [B1]
Level-marked (5–6 marks).

questions.prompt:
A sports drink advert claims that 'athletes who drink our product run 10 % faster'. The claim is based on 8 athletes who chose to drink it.

Evaluate the claim. (6)
questions.solution:
Very small sample of 8 [B1]
Self-selected — not random; may be fitter / more motivated [B1]
No control / placebo group [B1]
Not blind — expectations may affect performance [B1]
Other variables (training, diet) not controlled [B1]
Funded by the company — possible bias; not peer reviewed [B1]
Level-marked (5–6 marks).

questions.prompt: Discuss the arguments for and against banning performance-enhancing drugs in sport. (6)
questions.solution:
For a ban: unfair advantage over clean athletes [B1]
Health risks — e.g. heart disease, liver damage, infertility [B1]
Pressure on young athletes to use them [B1]
Against: athletes' right to choose / informed adults [B1]
Testing is expensive and some drugs undetectable [B1]
A level playing field if everyone could use them / medical supervision [B1]
Level-marked (5–6 marks).

questions.prompt:
The inner sphere of ferritin has a volume of 268 nm³. It holds 4500 iron ions, each occupying 9.04 × 10⁻⁴ nm³.

Calculate the unoccupied volume. (3)
hints: Total volume of iron ions first.

questions.prompt: A spherical vesicle has a radius of 50 nm. Calculate its volume in µm³ (V = 4/3 πr³). (3)
A protein molecule of 268 nm³ contains 4500 metal ions of 0.002 nm³ each. Calculate the percentage of the volume filled by ions. (3)

Pondweed was placed in water baths at 10, 15, 20, 25 and 30 °C, and the oxygen concentration of the water was measured over time.

(i) Identify the independent variable, the dependent variable and one control variable. (3)
(ii) Identify one variable that might not have been controlled. (1)
hints: What was changed? What was measured?
questions.solution:
(i) Independent: temperature [B1]
Dependent: oxygen concentration / rate of oxygen production [B1]
Control: light intensity / CO₂ concentration / mass of pondweed / volume of water [B1]
(ii) e.g. CO₂ concentration falling / light from the room / age of plant [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how to control light intensity, temperature and CO₂ in an investigation into photosynthesis of pondweed. (4)
questions.solution:
Light: same lamp at a fixed distance in a darkened room [B1]
Use a heat shield / water bath to keep temperature constant [B1]
Add the same concentration of sodium hydrogencarbonate as a CO₂ source [B1]
Use the same species, mass and length of pondweed [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between repeatability, reproducibility and validity. (4)
questions.solution:
Repeatable: similar results when the same person repeats it with the same method [B1]
Reproducible: similar results when done by others / with different equipment [B1]
Valid: the investigation measures what it claims to, with variables controlled [B1]
Repeating and calculating means / identifying anomalies improves confidence [B1]

questions.prompt:
In an osmometer, a liquid rose in a capillary tube from 10.5 mm to 26.5 mm. Each reading was made with a ruler accurate to ±0.5 mm.

(i) Calculate the percentage uncertainty in the change in height. (2)
(ii) Suggest what the rise shows about the solutions inside and outside the membrane. (2)
hints: Two readings, so double the uncertainty.
questions.solution:
(i) Change = 16.0 mm; uncertainty = ±1.0 mm [M1]
1.0 ÷ 16.0 × 100 = 6.25 % [A1]
(ii) Water moved into the tube by osmosis [B1]
So the solution inside had a lower water potential (more concentrated) than outside [B1]

questions.prompt:
A balance reads to ±0.01 g. A potato cylinder weighed 2.45 g before and 2.21 g after soaking.

Calculate the percentage uncertainty in the change in mass and suggest how to reduce it. (4)
questions.solution:
Change = 0.24 g; uncertainty = ±0.02 g [M1]
0.02 ÷ 0.24 × 100 = 8.3 % [A1]
Use larger cylinders / longer time, so the change is larger [B1]
Use a more precise balance (±0.001 g) [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between random and systematic errors, with an example of each. (4)
questions.solution:
Random errors vary unpredictably between readings [B1]
e.g. reading a meniscus inconsistently / not blotting cylinders equally [B1]
Systematic errors shift all readings by the same amount / in the same direction [B1]
e.g. a balance not zeroed / a miscalibrated thermometer [B1]

questions.prompt:
A student grew one plant in fertiliser A (grew 20.3 cm) and one in fertiliser B (grew 15.4 cm) and concluded A is better.

Describe and explain improvements to give more confidence in the conclusion. (6)
questions.solution:
Use many plants per fertiliser [B1]
Use clones (same genotype) so genetic variation doesn't affect results [B1]
Control light, temperature, water, volume / concentration of fertiliser, pot size [B1]
Include a control with no fertiliser [B1]
Measure height accurately over a set time / measure dry mass instead [B1]
Calculate means and SD, and use a t-test [B1]
Level-marked (5–6 marks).

questions.prompt: Plan an investigation into the effect of nitrate concentration on the growth of duckweed. (6)
questions.solution:
Set up containers with a range of nitrate concentrations (e.g. 0, 2, 4, 6, 8 g dm⁻³) [B1]
Same number of duckweed plants / fronds in each [B1]
Same volume, light, temperature [B1]
Count fronds every few days for two weeks [B1]
Repeat each concentration at least 3 times [B1]
Calculate mean growth rate and plot against concentration [B1]
Level-marked (5–6 marks).

questions.prompt: Explain how a t-test would be used to compare plant growth with two fertilisers. (6)
questions.solution:
Null hypothesis: no significant difference in mean growth [B1]
Calculate the mean and standard deviation for each group [B1]
Calculate t [B1]
Degrees of freedom = n₁ + n₂ − 2 [B1]
Compare with the critical value at p = 0.05 [B1]
If t is greater, reject the null hypothesis — difference is significant [B1]
Level-marked (5–6 marks).

questions.prompt: Chloroplast counts in seven cells: 13, 14, 13, 21, 14, 13, 17. Give the mean, median and mode. (1)
questions.solution: Mean 15, median 14, mode 13 [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the statistical test used to compare the mean number of chloroplasts in leaves from high-light and low-light areas. (1)
questions.solution: Student's t-test (unpaired) [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why the median may be a better average than the mean for data containing an anomaly. (1)
questions.solution: The median is not affected by extreme values / anomalies, while the mean is pulled towards them [B1]

questions.prompt:
(i) Describe how to make 30 cm³ of 0.8, 0.6 and 0.4 mol dm⁻³ sucrose solutions from a 1.0 mol dm⁻³ stock. (3)
(ii) A weighing boat weighed 10.55 g empty and 44.78 g with sucrose, on a balance accurate to ±0.01 g. Calculate the percentage uncertainty in the mass of sucrose. (2)
questions.solution:
(i) 0.8: 24 cm³ stock + 6 cm³ water [B1]
0.6: 18 cm³ stock + 12 cm³ water [B1]
0.4: 12 cm³ stock + 18 cm³ water [B1]
(ii) Mass = 34.23 g; uncertainty = ±0.02 g [M1]
0.02 ÷ 34.23 × 100 = 0.058 % [A1]

questions.prompt:
(i) Calculate the mass of sucrose (Mr = 342) needed to make 250 cm³ of a 1.0 mol dm⁻³ solution. (2)
(ii) Describe how to carry out a serial dilution to make 0.1, 0.01 and 0.001 mol dm⁻³ solutions. (3)
questions.solution:
(i) 1.0 × 0.25 = 0.25 mol [M1]
0.25 × 342 = 85.5 g [A1]
(ii) Add 1 cm³ of stock to 9 cm³ water to make 0.1 [B1]
Mix, then take 1 cm³ of this into 9 cm³ water to make 0.01 [B1]
Repeat for 0.001 [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why a graduated pipette is better than a measuring cylinder for making dilutions, and calculate the percentage uncertainty of measuring 2.0 cm³ with a pipette accurate to ±0.05 cm³. (5)
questions.solution:
Pipette has finer graduations / is more precise [B1]
Smaller volumes can be measured accurately [B1]
Reduces errors in concentration [B1]
0.05 ÷ 2.0 × 100 [M1]
= 2.5 % [A1]

questions.prompt:
The lengths of 500 cod were recorded in classes 100–199 mm, 200–299 mm, up to 700–799 mm.

(i) Describe how to present these data. (5)
(ii) Explain why the distribution suggests that some variation in length is caused by the environment. (2)
questions.solution:
(i) Histogram (continuous data in classes) [B1]
Length on x-axis, frequency on y-axis, with labels and units [B1]
Bars touching, equal class widths [B1]
Sensible linear scale using most of the grid [B1]
Bars plotted accurately [B1]
(ii) Continuous variation / normal distribution [B1]
Continuous variation is influenced by many genes and the environment (e.g. food availability, temperature) [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the features of a normal distribution and explain how standard deviation describes it. (7)
questions.solution:
Symmetrical, bell-shaped curve [B1]
Mean, median and mode are equal [B1]
Most values near the mean, few at the extremes [B1]
Standard deviation measures the spread around the mean [B1]
About 68 % of values lie within ±1 SD [B1]
About 95 % within ±2 SD [B1]
Larger SD = more variation [B1]

questions.prompt: Five cod measured 410, 450, 470, 500 and 520 mm. Calculate the mean and the standard deviation, using SD = √[Σ(x − x̄)² ÷ (n − 1)]. (7)

Mean root length was 16.5 grid squares in IAA and 13.9 grid squares in water.

Calculate the percentage change to 2 significant figures. (2)
Shoot length fell from 24.0 mm in water to 18.6 mm in a high IAA concentration. Calculate the percentage change. (2)
Explain why using grid squares to measure root length introduces uncertainty, and suggest an improvement. (2)
questions.solution:
Only measures to the nearest grid square / curved roots hard to measure [B1]
Use thread along the root and measure with a ruler in mm / image analysis software [B1]

questions.prompt:
IAA concentrations used were 100, 10, 1, 0.1, 0.01, 0.001, 0.0001 and 0.00001 ppm.

(i) Describe how to plot percentage change in root length against IAA concentration. (4)
(ii) Outline how to make these solutions from a 100 ppm stock. (2)
(iii) Describe two precautions to make sure concentrations are accurate. (2)
(iv) Explain why this range is described as logarithmic. (1)
questions.solution:
(i) IAA concentration on the x-axis using a log scale / log₁₀ concentration [B1]
Percentage change on the y-axis, with positive and negative values [B1]
Axes labelled with units [B1]
Points plotted accurately and joined with straight lines [B1]
(ii) Serial dilution: 1 cm³ stock + 9 cm³ distilled water gives 10 ppm [B1]
Repeat using each new solution, mixing thoroughly [B1]
(iii) Use graduated pipettes / syringes; read at eye level [B1]
Use a fresh pipette for each concentration / mix well [B1]
(iv) Each concentration is ten times lower than the last [B1]

questions.prompt: Plan an investigation into the effect of gibberellin concentration on the growth of dwarf pea seedlings. (9)
questions.solution:
Grow dwarf pea seedlings of the same age / variety [B1]
Prepare a range of gibberellin concentrations by serial dilution [B1]
Include a control with water only [B1]
Apply the same volume to each plant (e.g. drop at the apical bud) [B1]
Control light, temperature, water, soil [B1]
Measure height / internode length at the start and after a set time [B1]
Use several plants per concentration [B1]
Calculate mean growth and percentage change [B1]
Plot against log concentration; apply a statistical test [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how to evaluate the quality of the data from an investigation into the effect of IAA on root growth. (9)
questions.solution:
Look at repeats — are they close together (precision)? [B1]
Calculate standard deviation / range for each concentration [B1]
Identify anomalies and suggest causes [B1]
Consider measurement uncertainty (grid squares vs mm) [B1]
Consider whether variables were controlled (temperature, seed age) [B1]
Check if sample size is large enough [B1]
Use a statistical test to check significance [B1]
Consider validity — does it measure the effect of IAA? [B1]
Suggest improvements and further work [B1]

questions.prompt:
Volumes of oxygen at 60 s for 20 a.u. were 78, 74 and 78 cm³ (mean 76.7). At 2 a.u., 4.8 cm³ was collected in the first 30 s.

(i) Calculate the standard deviation for the 20 a.u. results using SD = √[Σ(x − x̄)² ÷ (n − 1)]. (2)
(ii) Discuss what the SDs show about repeatability. (2)
(iii) Calculate the initial rate at 2 a.u., with units. (2)
(iv) Suggest two reasons why the volume collected may be less than the volume produced. (2)
questions.solution:
(i) Σ(x − x̄)² = 1.69 + 7.29 + 1.69 = 10.67 [M1]
√(10.67 ÷ 2) = 2.31 [A1]
(ii) SD small compared with the mean, so results are repeatable [B1]
Large SDs at some concentrations would show less repeatability / overlap of ranges [B1]
(iii) 4.8 ÷ 30 = 0.16 [M1]
cm³ s⁻¹ [A1]
(iv) Some oxygen dissolves in water / leaks from joints [B1]
Gas produced before the bung was inserted [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how to find the initial rate of an enzyme reaction from a graph of product volume against time, and why initial rates are used to compare conditions. (8)
questions.solution:
Plot volume of product against time [B1]
Draw a tangent to the curve at t = 0 [B1]
Gradient = change in y ÷ change in x [B1]
Give units (e.g. cm³ s⁻¹) [B1]
Initial rate is used because substrate concentration is known / highest at the start [B1]
Later the substrate is used up, so rate falls [B1]
Product may inhibit the enzyme later [B1]
So initial rates allow a fair comparison [B1]

questions.prompt:
A gas syringe reads to ±0.5 cm³ and a stopwatch to ±0.1 s.

(i) Calculate the percentage uncertainty in measuring 20.0 cm³ of gas. (2)
(ii) Explain why reaction time is often a bigger source of error than the stopwatch. (2)
(iii) Explain two ways of reducing uncertainty. (4)
questions.solution:
(i) 0.5 ÷ 20.0 × 100 [M1]
= 2.5 % [A1]
(ii) Human reaction time is around 0.2–0.3 s [B1]
Larger than the stopwatch resolution [B1]
(iii) Measure larger volumes / longer times, so uncertainty is a smaller percentage [B1]
Because uncertainty is fixed in absolute terms [B1]
Use more precise apparatus / data logger [B1]
Removing human reaction time errors [B1]

questions.prompt:
(i) Suggest why immobilised yeast is more expensive to use than immobilised invertase. (1)
(ii) Outline a valid method to compare the ability of immobilised invertase and immobilised yeast to hydrolyse sucrose, using a glass column. (6)
questions.solution:
(i) Yeast uses some of the glucose / needs nutrients and conditions to stay alive [B1]
(ii) Make beads by dropping sodium alginate + invertase (or yeast) into calcium chloride solution [B1]
Pack the same volume of beads into identical columns [B1]
Pour the same volume and concentration of sucrose solution through at the same temperature [B1]
Control the flow rate (tap) [B1]
Test samples of the outflow for glucose using test strips / Benedict's + colorimeter [B1]
Repeat and compare glucose concentration produced [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how to make alginate beads containing lactase and use them to produce lactose-free milk. (7)
questions.solution:
Mix lactase with sodium alginate solution [B1]
Drop the mixture from a syringe into calcium chloride solution [B1]
Beads form; rinse with distilled water [B1]
Pack beads into a column with a tap [B1]
Pour milk through the column [B1]
Test the output for glucose (test strips) to show lactose is hydrolysed [B1]
Slower flow rate gives more time for reaction [B1]

questions.prompt: Plan an investigation into the effect of temperature on the activity of free and immobilised lactase. (7)
questions.solution:
Prepare equal amounts of free lactase and lactase in alginate beads [B1]
Incubate each with the same volume of milk / lactose solution in water baths at a range of temperatures [B1]
Pre-equilibrate solutions to temperature [B1]
After a set time, measure glucose concentration (test strip / colorimeter) [B1]
For free enzyme, stop the reaction (boil) before testing [B1]
Repeat each temperature and calculate means [B1]
Plot activity against temperature for each and compare optimum / stability [B1]

questions.prompt: Give two structural features of chloroplasts found in all photosynthetic eukaryotes. (2)
questions.solution:
Double membrane / envelope; thylakoid membranes [B1]
Own circular DNA and 70S ribosomes / stroma / starch grains [B1]

questions.prompt: Compare the ultrastructure of a typical plant cell and a typical animal cell. (2)
questions.solution:
Plant cells have a cellulose cell wall, chloroplasts and a large permanent vacuole [B1]
Animal cells have centrioles and no cell wall / small temporary vacuoles [B1]

questions.prompt: Give two structures found in prokaryotic cells but not eukaryotic cells. (2)
questions.solution:
Peptidoglycan (murein) cell wall / capsule [B1]
Plasmids / pili / naked circular DNA / mesosomes / 70S ribosomes in cytoplasm [B1]

questions.prompt: Which of these is not found in a chloroplast: cristae, DNA, ribosomes, thylakoids? (1)
questions.solution: Cristae [B1]

questions.prompt: Name one structure found in both mitochondria and chloroplasts. (1)
questions.solution: Circular DNA / 70S ribosomes / double membrane [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the organelle that forms the spindle in animal cells. (1)
questions.solution: Centrioles [B1]

questions.prompt:
(i) Give three functions of the cytoskeleton. (3)
(ii) Suggest how a mutation in a gene for a cytoskeleton protein could cause disease of the nervous system. (2)
questions.solution:
(i) Three of: maintains cell shape / support; moves organelles and vesicles; forms spindle fibres in division; cell movement (cilia, flagella); anchors organelles [B1 B1 B1]
(ii) Faulty protein so microtubules don't form properly [B1]
Vesicles / neurotransmitters / organelles can't be transported along long axons, so neurones don't function or die [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the structure and functions of microtubules and microfilaments. (5)
questions.solution:
Microtubules are hollow tubes made of tubulin [B1]
Form spindle fibres, cilia and flagella; tracks for transporting vesicles [B1]
Microfilaments are made of actin [B1]
Allow cell movement / cytokinesis / changes in shape [B1]
Intermediate filaments give mechanical strength [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the structure of cilia and explain how they function in the airways. (5)
questions.solution:
Cilia are extensions of the cell membrane containing microtubules [B1]
In a 9 + 2 arrangement [B1]
Microtubules slide past each other using ATP, making the cilia beat [B1]
Beat in a coordinated wave [B1]
Move mucus (with trapped pathogens and dust) up out of the airways [B1]

questions.prompt:
(i) Give three properties of cellulose that make it suitable for plant cell walls. (3)
(ii) Explain whether the cellulose-digesting enzymes of gut bacteria act inside or outside the bacterial cells. (1)
questions.solution:
(i) High tensile strength [B1]
Insoluble / not digested by most organisms [B1]
Freely permeable to water / forms microfibrils with hydrogen bonds [B1]
(ii) Extracellularly — cellulose molecules are too large to enter bacterial cells [B1]

questions.prompt: Compare the structures of cellulose and starch. (4)
questions.solution:
Cellulose made of β-glucose; starch of α-glucose [B1]
Cellulose: alternate glucose units inverted, forming straight chains [B1]
Starch: amylose coiled, amylopectin branched (1,6 bonds) [B1]
Cellulose chains form microfibrils with hydrogen bonds; starch forms compact granules [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why starch is a good storage molecule but cellulose is a good structural molecule. (4)
questions.solution:
Starch is compact, so stores much glucose in a small space [B1]
Starch is easily hydrolysed (branches give many ends) [B1]
Cellulose forms strong microfibrils held by hydrogen bonds [B1]
Cellulose is hard to hydrolyse, so it lasts [B1]

questions.prompt:
Chitin is a polymer of β-glucose with an acetylamine group in place of one OH group, with alternate monomers inverted and joined by 1,4 glycosidic bonds.

Give two similarities and two differences between chitin and glycogen. (4)
questions.solution:
Similarity: both are polysaccharides / polymers of glucose-based monomers [B1]
Similarity: both have 1,4 glycosidic bonds / are insoluble [B1]
Difference: chitin is β-based and unbranched; glycogen is α-glucose and highly branched [B1]
Difference: chitin contains nitrogen; it is structural rather than a store [B1]

questions.prompt: Compare amylopectin and glycogen. (4)
questions.solution:
Both are polymers of α-glucose [B1]
Both have 1,4 and 1,6 glycosidic bonds [B1]
Glycogen is more highly branched [B1]
Amylopectin is in plants (starch); glycogen in animals and fungi [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain what is meant by monomers and polymers, with two examples of each. (4)
questions.solution:
Monomers are small units that join to form polymers [B1]
Examples: glucose, amino acids, nucleotides [B1]
Polymers are long chains of repeating monomers joined by condensation reactions [B1]
Examples: starch / cellulose, proteins, DNA [B1]

questions.prompt: Give two properties of collagen that make it suitable for tendons. (1)
questions.solution: Strong (high tensile strength), flexible and insoluble [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the fibrous protein found in hair and nails. (1)
questions.solution: Keratin [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the fibrous protein that allows the walls of arteries to stretch and recoil. (1)
questions.solution: Elastin [B1]

questions.prompt:
(i) Name one food molecule that cannot be detected using biuret, Benedict's, iodine or the emulsion test. (1)
(ii) Give the result of the biuret test when protein is present. (1)
(iii) Explain how a colorimeter could improve the Benedict's test. (1)
questions.solution:
(i) Non-reducing sugars (e.g. sucrose) without hydrolysis / nucleic acids [B1]
(ii) Blue to purple / lilac [B1]
(iii) Gives a quantitative measure of colour / absorbance, so the concentration can be found from a calibration curve [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the test for non-reducing sugars. (3)
questions.solution:
Do a Benedict's test first — stays blue [B1]
Boil a new sample with dilute HCl, then neutralise with sodium hydrogencarbonate [B1]
Heat with Benedict's — brick-red precipitate shows non-reducing sugar [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why glucose test strips are useful for testing the urine of diabetic patients. (3)
questions.solution:
Contain the enzyme glucose oxidase, specific to glucose [B1]
Colour change can be compared with a chart to give the concentration [B1]
Quick, cheap and easy to use at home [B1]

questions.prompt:
Rubredoxin is a small protein with an iron ion held in place by the sulfur atoms of four cysteine residues.

Explain what is meant by a conjugated protein, using rubredoxin as an example. (3)
questions.solution:
A protein with a non-protein (prosthetic) group attached [B1]
In rubredoxin the prosthetic group is the iron ion [B1]
Held by bonds to sulfur atoms in the R groups of cysteine [B1]

questions.prompt: Give two examples of conjugated proteins and name their prosthetic groups. (3)
questions.solution:
Haemoglobin — haem group (containing Fe²⁺) [B1]
Catalase — haem group [B1]
Glycoproteins — carbohydrate group [B1]

questions.prompt: Give the roles of three inorganic ions in living organisms. (3)
questions.solution:
Fe²⁺ — part of haemoglobin, carries oxygen [B1]
PO₄³⁻ — part of nucleotides / ATP / phospholipids [B1]
Ca²⁺ — nerve impulse transmission / muscle contraction / bones [B1]
Na⁺ / K⁺ — nerve impulses / co-transport [B1]
Any 3 — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt:
Rubredoxin is a single polypeptide with one iron ion. Haemoglobin has four polypeptides and four haem groups.

(i) State two similarities between their structures. (2)
(ii) State two differences, other than secondary and tertiary structure. (2)
questions.solution:
(i) Both are globular / conjugated proteins [B1]
Both contain iron [B1]
(ii) Haemoglobin has quaternary structure (4 polypeptides); rubredoxin has one [B1]
Haemoglobin's iron is in haem groups; rubredoxin's iron is bound directly to cysteines / different number of iron ions [B1]

questions.prompt: Compare globular and fibrous proteins. (4)
questions.solution:
Globular proteins are compact and spherical; fibrous are long strands [B1]
Globular are usually soluble; fibrous are insoluble [B1]
Globular have metabolic roles (enzymes, haemoglobin, hormones); fibrous have structural roles (collagen, keratin) [B1]
Fibrous have repetitive amino acid sequences; globular are less regular [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how the tertiary structure of a globular protein makes it soluble. (4)
questions.solution:
R groups can be hydrophilic (polar) or hydrophobic (non-polar) [B1]
Hydrophobic R groups point inwards, away from water [B1]
Hydrophilic R groups face outwards [B1]
So water molecules can surround the protein [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how hydrophobic and hydrophilic interactions help a protein such as ferritin form a sphere. (1)
questions.solution: Hydrophobic R groups cluster away from water and hydrophilic R groups face the surrounding (and inner) water, causing folding into a sphere [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the type of bond that forms between two cysteine R groups. (1)
questions.solution: Disulfide bridge (bond) [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the bond formed between oppositely charged R groups. (1)
questions.solution: Ionic bond [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how the density of water and ice helps aquatic organisms survive. (3)
questions.solution:
Ice is less dense than liquid water, so it floats [B1]
Forms an insulating layer on top [B1]
Water underneath does not freeze, so organisms survive [B1]
Water is dense enough to support / provide buoyancy for organisms [B1]
Any 3 — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt: Explain how cohesion and surface tension are important to living organisms. (3)
questions.solution:
Hydrogen bonds between water molecules cause cohesion [B1]
Water is pulled up xylem as a continuous column [B1]
Surface tension allows small organisms (pond skaters) to walk on water [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why water's high latent heat of vaporisation is useful for cooling. (3)
questions.solution:
Many hydrogen bonds must be broken for water to evaporate [B1]
So a lot of heat energy is removed [B1]
Evaporation of sweat / transpiration cools organisms with little water lost [B1]

questions.prompt:
A lipoprotein has a radius of 11 nm. Each phospholipid occupies 0.65 nm² of the surface.

Calculate the number of phospholipids on the outer surface (surface area = 4πr²). (2)
questions.solution:
Surface area = 4 × 3.14 × 11² = 1520 nm² [M1]
1520 ÷ 0.65 = 2338 phospholipids [A1]

questions.prompt: Calculate the surface area to volume ratio of a sphere of radius 3 µm. (2)
questions.solution:
SA = 113 µm²; V = 113 µm³ [M1]
Ratio = 1 : 1 (3 ÷ r) [A1]

questions.prompt: Explain how lipids help aquatic animals stay buoyant. (2)
questions.solution:
Lipids are less dense than water [B1]
So stores of fat / blubber help animals float / reduce energy needed to stay up [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe six roles of lipids in living organisms. (6)
questions.solution:
Energy store (triglycerides) — more energy per gram than carbohydrates [B1]
Phospholipids form cell membranes [B1]
Thermal insulation (subcutaneous fat / blubber) [B1]
Protection of organs (cushioning) [B1]
Waterproofing (waxy cuticle) [B1]
Steroid hormones / cholesterol in membranes / myelin sheath insulation [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the structure and roles of cholesterol. (6)
questions.solution:
Cholesterol is a lipid with four carbon rings (steroid) [B1]
Has a hydrophilic OH group and hydrophobic rings [B1]
Regulates membrane fluidity [B1]
Used to make steroid hormones (testosterone, oestrogen) [B1]
Used to make vitamin D [B1]
Used to make bile [B1]
Level-marked (5–6 marks).

questions.prompt: Compare the structures and properties of triglycerides, phospholipids and cholesterol. (6)
questions.solution:
Triglyceride: glycerol + 3 fatty acids, ester bonds [B1]
Non-polar / hydrophobic — energy storage [B1]
Phospholipid: glycerol + 2 fatty acids + phosphate [B1]
Hydrophilic head and hydrophobic tails — forms bilayers [B1]
Cholesterol: four-ring steroid, mostly hydrophobic with an OH group [B1]
All are insoluble in water [B1]
Level-marked (5–6 marks).

questions.prompt: Using a triglyceride as an example, explain what is meant by hydrolysis. (2)
questions.solution:
Breaking a bond by adding water [B1]
Ester bonds broken, releasing glycerol and three fatty acids (catalysed by lipase) [B1]

questions.prompt: Using a dipeptide as an example, explain what is meant by a condensation reaction. (2)
questions.solution:
Two molecules join, releasing a molecule of water [B1]
Amine group of one amino acid reacts with the carboxyl group of another, forming a peptide bond [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why unsaturated fats are liquid at room temperature while saturated fats are solid. (2)
questions.solution:
C=C double bonds in unsaturated fatty acids cause kinks in the chains [B1]
So molecules can't pack closely together, lowering the melting point [B1]

questions.prompt: Give one function of cholesterol in animal cells. (1)
questions.solution: Regulates membrane fluidity / precursor of steroid hormones, vitamin D or bile [B1]

questions.prompt: State the type of bond formed between glycerol and fatty acids in a triglyceride, and the type of reaction that forms it. (1)
questions.solution: Ester bond, formed by a condensation reaction [B1]

questions.prompt: Climbers carry chocolate (high in fat) rather than mint cake (almost pure sugar). Explain why. (1)
questions.solution: Fat releases about twice as much energy per gram as sugar, so less mass needs to be carried for the same energy [B1]

questions.prompt: Outline the properties of water, other than its thermal properties, that are essential for life. (6)
questions.solution:
Polar molecule — good solvent for ions and polar molecules, allowing transport and reactions [B1]
Cohesion between molecules (hydrogen bonds) — continuous columns in xylem [B1]
Surface tension — habitat for small organisms [B1]
Ice less dense than water — floats and insulates water below [B1]
Transparent — light reaches aquatic plants [B1]
Reactant in photosynthesis and hydrolysis; incompressible — hydrostatic skeletons / turgor [B1]
Level-marked (5–6 marks).

questions.prompt: Explain how hydrogen bonding gives water properties that are important to living things. (6)
questions.solution:
Water is polar — δ− oxygen, δ+ hydrogens [B1]
Hydrogen bonds form between neighbouring molecules [B1]
High specific heat capacity — stable aquatic temperatures [B1]
High latent heat of vaporisation — cooling by sweating / transpiration [B1]
Cohesion — transpiration stream [B1]
Liquid at room temperature — transport medium [B1]
Level-marked (5–6 marks).

questions.prompt: Explain the importance of water as a solvent in living organisms, with examples. (6)
questions.solution:
Polar water molecules surround ions and polar molecules, dissolving them [B1]
Metabolic reactions take place in solution in the cytoplasm [B1]
Blood plasma transports dissolved glucose, amino acids, ions, urea [B1]
Phloem sap carries dissolved sucrose [B1]
Waste products (urea) excreted in solution [B1]
Non-polar molecules don't dissolve, so membranes form barriers [B1]
Level-marked (5–6 marks).

questions.prompt: Which bonds hold the secondary structure of a protein? (1)
questions.solution: Hydrogen bonds between C=O and N–H groups [B1]

questions.prompt: Give one property of cellulose. (1)
questions.solution: Insoluble / high tensile strength / forms microfibrils [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the structure of glycogen. (1)
questions.solution: α-glucose joined by 1,4 and many 1,6 glycosidic bonds — highly branched [B1]

questions.prompt:
(i) Name the bond in the primary structure of a protein. (1)
(ii) Name the prosthetic group in haemoglobin. (1)
(iii) Give one feature that shows haemoglobin is a globular protein. (1)
questions.solution:
(i) Peptide bond [B1]
(ii) Haem group [B1]
(iii) Spherical / compact shape / soluble / hydrophilic R groups on the outside [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the structure of haemoglobin. (3)
questions.solution:
Four polypeptide chains — two α and two β (quaternary structure) [B1]
Each with a haem prosthetic group containing Fe²⁺ [B1]
Globular, with hydrophilic R groups on the outside so it is soluble [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how the shape of a protein is determined by its amino acid sequence. (3)
questions.solution:
The sequence determines where R groups are [B1]
R groups interact (hydrogen, ionic, disulfide, hydrophobic) [B1]
Determining how the polypeptide folds into a specific 3D shape [B1]

questions.prompt:
(i) Outline how to use a colorimeter and biuret reagent to find the protein concentration of a sample. (4)
(ii) State one alternative method. (1)
questions.solution:
(i) Make protein solutions of known concentration (e.g. using serial dilution) [B1]
Add the same volume of biuret reagent to each and the unknown [B1]
Measure absorbance with a colorimeter, zeroed with a blank, using a suitable filter [B1]
Plot a calibration curve and read the unknown's concentration [B1]
(ii) Biosensor / chromatography / Kjeldahl method / Bradford assay [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how thin layer chromatography can be used to identify the amino acids in a protein. (5)
questions.solution:
Hydrolyse the protein into amino acids (acid / protease) [B1]
Spot onto a pencil origin line on a TLC plate [B1]
Run in a solvent; remove before it reaches the top [B1]
Spray with ninhydrin to show amino acids [B1]
Calculate Rf values and compare with known amino acids [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how a biosensor measures blood glucose concentration. (5)
questions.solution:
Immobilised glucose oxidase on an electrode [B1]
Enzyme is specific to glucose [B1]
Glucose oxidised, producing an electric current [B1]
Current is proportional to glucose concentration [B1]
Gives a quick, accurate digital reading [B1]

questions.prompt:
(i) Describe the structure of α-glucose. (3)
(ii) Explain how the structure of glucose allows it to move from a plant cell to bacteria in a root nodule. (2)
questions.solution:
(i) Hexose — six carbons, five in a ring with an oxygen [B1]
Hydroxyl groups on carbons 1–4 and carbon 6 (CH₂OH) [B1]
In α-glucose, the OH on carbon 1 is below the ring [B1]
(ii) Small and soluble (polar OH groups form hydrogen bonds with water) [B1]
So it can be transported in solution and cross membranes through carrier proteins [B1]

questions.prompt: Compare the structures of glucose, ribose and deoxyribose. (5)
questions.solution:
Glucose is a hexose (6 C) [B1]
Ribose and deoxyribose are pentoses (5 C) [B1]
Deoxyribose has one less oxygen than ribose (H instead of OH on carbon 2) [B1]
Ribose is in RNA / ATP; deoxyribose in DNA [B1]
All are monosaccharides with ring structures and OH groups [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why sucrose rather than glucose is transported in the phloem of plants. (5)
questions.solution:
Sucrose is a disaccharide of glucose and fructose [B1]
It is non-reducing, so less reactive [B1]
Not used in respiration on the way [B1]
Highly soluble, so can be transported in solution [B1]
Hydrolysed by invertase at the sink to release monosaccharides [B1]

questions.prompt: Which pyrimidine base is found in RNA but not DNA? (1)
questions.solution: Uracil [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the two purine bases. (1)
questions.solution: Adenine and guanine [B1]

questions.prompt: State the three components of an RNA nucleotide. (1)
questions.solution: Ribose, a phosphate group and a nitrogenous base (A, U, C or G) [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the structure of ATP. (1)
questions.solution: Adenine, ribose and three phosphate groups [B1]

questions.prompt: Give two reasons why ATP is a suitable energy currency. (1)
questions.solution: Releases energy in small, manageable amounts / hydrolysed in one step / easily regenerated / soluble [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the enzyme that hydrolyses ATP. (1)
questions.solution: ATP hydrolase (ATPase) [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how a competitive inhibitor reduces the rate of an enzyme reaction. (1)
questions.solution: It has a similar shape to the substrate and binds to the active site, so fewer enzyme–substrate complexes form [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how a non-competitive inhibitor reduces the rate of an enzyme reaction. (1)
questions.solution: It binds to an allosteric site, changing the shape of the active site so the substrate can't bind [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why increasing substrate concentration reduces the effect of a competitive inhibitor but not a non-competitive inhibitor. (1)
questions.solution: More substrate out-competes a competitive inhibitor for the active site; a non-competitive inhibitor changes the active site, so extra substrate can't bind [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how increasing enzyme concentration affects a graph of rate against substrate concentration. (1)
questions.solution: The curve rises more steeply and levels off at a higher maximum rate (Vmax) [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why enzymes from organisms living in hot springs have a high optimum temperature. (1)
questions.solution: They have more bonds (e.g. disulfide / ionic) holding the tertiary structure, so they don't denature easily [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why the rate of an enzyme reaction is low at 5 °C but the enzyme is not denatured. (1)
questions.solution: Molecules have little kinetic energy, so fewer collisions / enzyme–substrate complexes; the active site shape is unchanged [B1]

questions.prompt: Give one example of an enzyme that acts extracellularly. (1)
questions.solution: Amylase / trypsin / thrombin (in blood clotting) [B1]

questions.prompt: Give one advantage of using immobilised enzymes in industry. (1)
questions.solution: Enzymes can be reused / product not contaminated with enzyme / more stable at higher temperatures [B1]

questions.prompt: Give one disadvantage of using immobilised enzymes. (1)
questions.solution: More expensive to set up / lower reaction rate as substrate has less access to active sites [B1]

questions.prompt:
Students measured oxygen released when potato cylinders were added to hydrogen peroxide at 2, 8 and 20 a.u.

(i) Identify the independent variable. (1)
(ii) Describe how to make 10 cm³ of 8 a.u. solution from a 20 a.u. stock. (2)
(iii) Suggest two reasons for using potato rather than liver. (2)
(iv) Suggest one precaution when preparing potato cylinders. (1)
questions.solution:
(i) Concentration of hydrogen peroxide [B1]
(ii) 4 cm³ of stock [B1]
+ 6 cm³ distilled water [B1]
(iii) Liver has very high catalase activity — reaction too fast to measure [B1]
Potato is cheaper / ethical / easier to cut into equal pieces [B1]
(iv) Same length / diameter / surface area, from the same potato [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how to measure the rate of oxygen production by catalase using a gas syringe or inverted measuring cylinder. (6)
questions.solution:
Set up a conical flask with a bung connected to a gas syringe / delivery tube into an inverted measuring cylinder of water [B1]
Add a fixed volume and concentration of H₂O₂ [B1]
Add potato pieces of the same mass / surface area and immediately close the bung [B1]
Record volume of oxygen every 30 s [B1]
Keep temperature and pH constant (water bath, buffer) [B1]
Repeat and calculate the initial rate from the gradient [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why catalase is important in cells and why it works so fast. (6)
questions.solution:
Hydrogen peroxide is a toxic by-product of metabolism [B1]
Catalase breaks it into water and oxygen [B1]
It is found in peroxisomes / most cells [B1]
Very high turnover number [B1]
Active site has a low activation energy for this reaction [B1]
Iron-containing haem group (prosthetic group / cofactor) [B1]

questions.prompt:
At 20 a.u., the volume of oxygen rose rapidly for 90 s, then levelled off at 120 cm³.

Explain these results. (3)
questions.solution:
Initially many substrate molecules, so many enzyme–substrate complexes — fast rate [B1]
As H₂O₂ is used up, fewer collisions, so rate slows [B1]
Levels off when all substrate is broken down — final volume depends on substrate amount [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why increasing substrate concentration increases the rate of reaction only up to a point. (3)
questions.solution:
More substrate gives more collisions / enzyme–substrate complexes [B1]
At high concentration all active sites are occupied (saturated) [B1]
Enzyme concentration becomes the limiting factor, so rate levels off (Vmax) [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between coenzymes, cofactors and prosthetic groups. (3)
questions.solution:
Cofactors are non-protein substances needed for enzyme activity (e.g. Cl⁻ for amylase) [B1]
Coenzymes are organic cofactors, often from vitamins (e.g. NAD, coenzyme A), that bind temporarily [B1]
Prosthetic groups are permanently bound cofactors (e.g. Zn²⁺ in carbonic anhydrase) [B1]

questions.prompt:
(i) Name one method of immobilising enzymes. (1)
(ii) Explain why immobilised enzymes may be less active than free enzymes. (2)
questions.solution:
(i) Entrapment in alginate beads / adsorption onto clay / covalent bonding / membrane separation [B1]
(ii) Substrate must diffuse into the matrix to reach enzymes, so fewer collisions [B1]
Binding may change the shape of the active site / block it [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why immobilised enzymes are often more stable at high temperatures. (3)
questions.solution:
The matrix holds the enzyme in place [B1]
Restricts movement / unfolding of the polypeptide [B1]
So the tertiary structure is less easily denatured [B1]

questions.prompt: Give three industrial uses of immobilised enzymes. (3)
questions.solution:
Glucose isomerase — making fructose syrup [B1]
Lactase — making lactose-free milk [B1]
Penicillin acylase — making semi-synthetic penicillins / aminoacylase — pure amino acids [B1]

questions.prompt:
(i) State and explain one property of cholesterol that contributes to membrane stability. (2)
(ii) Outline the roles of membranes within cells. (2)
questions.solution:
(i) Cholesterol is partly hydrophobic and fits between phospholipid tails [B1]
Reduces movement / fluidity, so the membrane is more stable [B1]
(ii) Compartmentalise the cell / keep enzymes separate (e.g. lysosomes) [B1]
Provide surfaces for reactions (cristae, thylakoids) / form vesicles for transport [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the fluid mosaic model of membrane structure. (4)
questions.solution:
Phospholipid bilayer with hydrophilic heads outwards [B1]
Intrinsic proteins span the bilayer; extrinsic proteins on the surface [B1]
Cholesterol between phospholipids regulates fluidity [B1]
Glycoproteins and glycolipids act as receptors / recognition sites; components move freely [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe endocytosis and exocytosis. (4)
questions.solution:
Endocytosis: membrane surrounds material, forming a vesicle that enters the cell [B1]
e.g. phagocytosis of bacteria / pinocytosis of liquids [B1]
Exocytosis: vesicles fuse with the cell membrane, releasing contents [B1]
Both require ATP (bulk transport), e.g. secretion of hormones / enzymes [B1]

questions.prompt:
(i) Give three assumptions made in using absorbance of the surrounding solution to measure damage to beetroot membranes by ethanol. (3)
(ii) Give two variables, other than temperature, to control. (2)
hints: Pigment leaks only from damaged membranes.
questions.solution:
(i) Pigment only leaks out if membranes are damaged [B1]
Absorbance is proportional to pigment concentration [B1]
Cutting releases pigment equally from all samples (so rinsing is needed) [B1]
(ii) Size / surface area of beetroot pieces [B1]
Volume of ethanol solution / time left in solution [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how to investigate the effect of temperature on beetroot membrane permeability. (5)
questions.solution:
Cut equal-sized beetroot cylinders and rinse to remove pigment from cut cells [B1]
Place in equal volumes of distilled water in water baths at a range of temperatures [B1]
Leave for a set time [B1]
Measure absorbance of the solution with a colorimeter (blue-green filter), zeroed with water [B1]
Repeat and plot absorbance against temperature [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain the effect of increasing temperature and of ethanol on cell membranes. (5)
questions.solution:
Higher temperature gives phospholipids more kinetic energy, increasing fluidity / gaps [B1]
Membrane proteins denature, leaving gaps [B1]
So permeability increases and pigment leaks out [B1]
Ethanol dissolves the phospholipids / is a lipid solvent [B1]
Higher ethanol concentration causes more damage [B1]

questions.prompt: Define osmosis. (2)
questions.solution:
Net movement of water molecules from a region of higher water potential to lower water potential [B1]
Across a partially permeable membrane [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain what is meant by water potential, and why pure water has a water potential of zero. (2)
questions.solution:
Water potential is the tendency of water molecules to move from one area to another (kPa) [B1]
Pure water has the highest water potential (0); adding solutes makes it negative [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between diffusion and facilitated diffusion. (2)
questions.solution:
Diffusion is passive net movement down a concentration gradient directly through the bilayer (small / non-polar molecules) [B1]
Facilitated diffusion is also passive but uses channel or carrier proteins (large / polar molecules / ions) [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain the importance of osmosis in supporting non-woody plants. (3)
questions.solution:
Water enters cells by osmosis, as the cytoplasm / vacuole has a lower water potential [B1]
Cells become turgid, with the cytoplasm pushing against the cell wall [B1]
Turgid cells press against each other, supporting the stem and leaves; without water plants wilt [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe what happens to a plant cell placed in a concentrated sucrose solution. (3)
questions.solution:
Solution has a lower water potential than the cell [B1]
Water leaves the cell by osmosis; vacuole and cytoplasm shrink [B1]
Cell membrane pulls away from the wall — plasmolysis; cell becomes flaccid [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why it is important that the water potential of blood plasma is kept constant. (3)
questions.solution:
If plasma water potential is too high, water enters cells by osmosis and they may burst (haemolysis) [B1]
If too low, water leaves cells and they shrink (crenation) [B1]
Animal cells have no cell wall, so cells can't function properly [B1]

questions.prompt:
Cylinders of potato, carrot and courgette were placed in sucrose solutions of 0.0–0.8 mol dm⁻³. The concentration giving 0 % change in mass was 0.3 mol dm⁻³ for potato, 0.4 for carrot and 0.25 for courgette.

(i) Explain why percentage change in mass was calculated. (2)
(ii) Suggest a practical error that could cause one potato replicate to be anomalous, and its effect. (2)
(iii) Identify which vegetable's cells had the highest solute concentration, and justify your answer. (3)
questions.solution:
(i) Cylinders had different starting masses [B1]
So percentage change allows fair comparison [B1]
(ii) e.g. not blotting excess solution before weighing, giving a higher final mass [B1]
or the cylinder was a different size / left out to dry, giving a lower mass [B1]
(iii) Carrot [B1]
No change in mass at the highest sucrose concentration (0.4 mol dm⁻³) [B1]
So its cells had the lowest water potential / most solute [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how you would find the water potential of potato cells, using a range of sucrose solutions. (7)
questions.solution:
Make a range of sucrose solutions by serial / proportional dilution [B1]
Cut potato cylinders of the same size with a cork borer [B1]
Blot dry and weigh each, then place in a solution [B1]
Leave for a set time (e.g. 24 h) at constant temperature [B1]
Remove, blot and reweigh; calculate percentage change in mass [B1]
Plot percentage change against concentration [B1]
Read off where the line crosses zero; use a table to convert to water potential [B1]

questions.prompt:
(i) Describe how to make 10 cm³ of 0.2, 0.4 and 0.6 mol dm⁻³ sucrose solutions from a 1.0 mol dm⁻³ stock. (3)
(ii) Explain why the cylinders were blotted before weighing. (2)
(iii) Explain why the experiment should be repeated. (2)
questions.solution:
(i) 0.2: 2 cm³ stock + 8 cm³ water [B1]
0.4: 4 cm³ stock + 6 cm³ water [B1]
0.6: 6 cm³ stock + 4 cm³ water [B1]
(ii) To remove surface liquid [B1]
So only the change in water inside the cells is measured [B1]
(iii) To identify anomalies [B1]
And calculate a mean, improving reliability [B1]

questions.prompt:
(i) Potato cylinders in 0.6 mol dm⁻³ sucrose changed length by −4 %, −5 %, +3 % and −5 %. Identify the anomalous result. (1)
(ii) Give one variable to control in this experiment and a reason. (2)
questions.solution:
(i) +3 % [B1]
(ii) e.g. temperature / time in solution / initial cylinder size / same potato [B1]
Reason, e.g. temperature affects the rate of osmosis [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why potato cylinders got longer in distilled water and shorter in 0.8 mol dm⁻³ sucrose. (3)
questions.solution:
In distilled water, water potential outside was higher, so water entered by osmosis — cells became turgid and longer [B1]
In 0.8 mol dm⁻³ sucrose, water potential outside was lower, so water left cells [B1]
Cells became flaccid / plasmolysed, so cylinders shortened [B1]

questions.prompt: Give three ways to improve the reliability of a potato cylinder osmosis experiment. (3)
questions.solution:
Repeat each concentration at least three times and calculate a mean [B1]
Cut all cylinders from the same potato with the same cork borer [B1]
Blot each cylinder the same way / measure mass rather than length / leave longer [B1]

questions.prompt: Name three types of animal tissue and give a function of each. (3)
questions.solution:
Squamous / ciliated epithelium — lining / moving mucus [B1]
Muscle — contraction [B1]
Cartilage / connective tissue — support / joining; nervous tissue — transmitting impulses [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how the structures of three specialised cells are related to their functions. (3)
questions.solution:
Sperm: flagellum for movement, acrosome enzymes, many mitochondria [B1]
Root hair cell: long extension for large surface area [B1]
Guard cells: thicker inner wall so they bend to open stomata / palisade cells with many chloroplasts [B1]

questions.prompt:
Why are stem cells a possible treatment for diseases that damage many types of tissue?

Choose one answer.

A  They can be taken from any adult tissue
B  They are cheaper than drugs
C  They can differentiate into many types of specialised cell
D  They raise no ethical concerns (1)
hints: What is special about stem cells?
questions.solution: C — they can differentiate into many types of specialised cell. [B1]

questions.prompt: Give one source of stem cells for medical use that avoids destroying embryos. (1)
questions.solution: Umbilical cord blood / adult bone marrow / induced pluripotent stem cells [B1]

questions.prompt: Give one disease that might be treated using stem cells. (1)
hints: Damaged tissue that does not regenerate.
questions.solution: e.g. type 1 diabetes / Parkinson's disease / Alzheimer's / spinal cord injury / heart disease [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the blood cell with a lobed nucleus and granular cytoplasm that carries out phagocytosis. (1)
questions.solution: Neutrophil [B1]

questions.prompt: Give one feature of an erythrocyte that adapts it for carrying oxygen. (1)
questions.solution: Biconcave shape (large surface area) / no nucleus (more room for haemoglobin) / flexible [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the white blood cell with a large round nucleus that fills most of the cell. (1)
questions.solution: Lymphocyte [B1]

questions.prompt: Are haematopoietic stem cells in bone marrow totipotent, pluripotent or multipotent? (1)
questions.solution: Multipotent [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the type of stem cell found in the inner cell mass of a blastocyst. (1)
hints: Can form any body cell but not placenta.
questions.solution: Pluripotent [B1]

questions.prompt: Give the meaning of totipotent. (1)
questions.solution: Able to differentiate into any type of cell, including placental cells [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why meristem cells can become xylem vessels but xylem vessels cannot become any other cell. (1)
hints: Living and unspecialised vs dead and specialised.
questions.solution: Meristem cells are living and unspecialised; mature xylem vessels are dead / lignified, specialised cells [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the tissue between xylem and phloem in a vascular bundle that produces new xylem and phloem cells. (1)
questions.solution: Cambium [B1]

questions.prompt: Name two places where meristems are found in a plant. (1)
questions.solution: Two of: root tips, shoot tips (apical meristems), cambium / lateral meristem [B1]

questions.prompt: Compare skeletal, cardiac and involuntary (smooth) muscle. (3)
questions.solution:
Skeletal: voluntary (conscious control), multinucleate, contracts rapidly [B1]
Cardiac: myogenic, branched interconnected fibres with intercalated discs [B1]
Involuntary: single nucleus per cell, spindle-shaped, slow sustained contraction, no striations [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why cardiac muscle cells are connected by intercalated discs. (3)
questions.solution:
Intercalated discs contain gap junctions [B1]
Allow ions / impulses to pass rapidly between cells [B1]
So the heart contracts in a coordinated way [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the structure of a skeletal muscle fibre. (3)
questions.solution:
Long multinucleate cell surrounded by the sarcolemma, with T-tubules [B1]
Contains many myofibrils made of actin and myosin, arranged in sarcomeres [B1]
Many mitochondria and extensive sarcoplasmic reticulum storing Ca²⁺ [B1]

questions.prompt:
Mouse embryonic stem cells (ESCs) treated with growth factors became thyroid tissue that produced thyroxine when transplanted into mice without a thyroid.

(i) Explain what is meant by pluripotent. (2)
(ii) Evaluate the conclusion that the growth factors caused the ESCs to become functional thyroid tissue, given that untreated ESCs produced no thyroxine and the treated group's thyroxine levels varied widely. (3)
(iii) Give one reason for and one reason against using human iPSCs rather than ESCs to treat hypothyroidism. (2)
questions.solution:
(i) Able to differentiate into almost any cell type [B1]
But not extra-embryonic tissue (placenta) [B1]
(ii) Supports: thyroxine produced only with growth factors (control group produced none) [B1]
But wide variation — not all transplants worked / small sample [B1]
Mice not humans; no statistical test; long-term function unknown [B1]
(iii) For: patient's own cells — no rejection, no embryos destroyed [B1]
Against: iPSCs may carry mutations / risk of tumours / less tested [B1]

questions.prompt: Discuss the potential uses and ethical issues of stem cells in medicine. (7)
questions.solution:
Can replace damaged cells, e.g. for type 1 diabetes, Parkinson's, spinal injury [B1]
Bone marrow transplants already treat leukaemia [B1]
Drug testing on stem-cell-derived tissues [B1]
Embryonic stem cells involve destroying embryos — ethical objection [B1]
Adult / umbilical / iPS cells reduce ethical concerns [B1]
Risks: rejection, tumour formation [B1]
Cost and availability [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the differentiation of stem cells into erythrocytes and neutrophils, and explain how each is adapted to its function. (7)
questions.solution:
Both arise from multipotent stem cells in bone marrow [B1]
Different genes switched on in each [B1]
Erythrocytes lose their nucleus and organelles — more space for haemoglobin [B1]
Biconcave shape gives large SA for oxygen diffusion [B1]
Neutrophils have a lobed nucleus, allowing them to squeeze through capillary walls [B1]
Many lysosomes for digesting pathogens [B1]
Can change shape to engulf pathogens [B1]

questions.prompt:
(i) State two roles of mitosis other than asexual reproduction. (1)
(ii) Explain why plants use mitosis rather than meiosis for asexual reproduction. (2)
(iii) Suggest why bacteria cannot reproduce by mitosis. (2)
hints: Bacteria have no nucleus or spindle.
questions.solution:
(i) Growth and repair / replacement of cells [B1]
(ii) Mitosis produces genetically identical diploid cells [B1]
Meiosis halves the chromosome number and produces variation, so offspring would not be clones / would be haploid [B1]
(iii) Bacteria are prokaryotes with no nucleus / no linear chromosomes [B1]
No spindle / no centrioles — they divide by binary fission [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the stages of mitosis. (5)
questions.solution:
Prophase: chromosomes condense; nuclear envelope breaks down; spindle forms [B1]
Metaphase: chromosomes line up on the equator, attached to spindle fibres by centromeres [B1]
Anaphase: centromeres divide; sister chromatids pulled to opposite poles [B1]
Telophase: chromatids reach the poles; nuclear envelopes reform; chromosomes uncoil [B1]
Cytokinesis divides the cytoplasm, giving two identical cells [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how the cell cycle is regulated by checkpoints. (5)
questions.solution:
G1 checkpoint: checks cell size, nutrients, DNA damage before replication [B1]
G2 checkpoint: checks DNA has replicated correctly / is undamaged [B1]
Metaphase (spindle) checkpoint: checks chromosomes are attached to spindle [B1]
If problems are found, the cycle stops / DNA repaired / apoptosis triggered [B1]
Prevents uncontrolled division — failure can lead to cancer [B1]

questions.prompt:
A spirometer trace of a pregnant woman showed that oxygen was used at 0.016 dm³ s⁻¹. The normal value for women is about 0.020 dm³ s⁻¹. A student claimed pregnancy reduces oxygen uptake by up to 20 %.

Evaluate the claim. (3)
questions.solution:
Decrease = 0.004 ÷ 0.020 × 100 = 20 % — consistent with the claim [B1]
But only one woman measured — not representative [B1]
Normal value is approximate / no repeats / other factors (fitness, size) not controlled [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how a spirometer trace is used to measure tidal volume, breathing rate and vital capacity. (3)
questions.solution:
Tidal volume — difference between a peak and trough during normal breathing [B1]
Breathing rate — number of peaks per minute [B1]
Vital capacity — height of the largest breath (maximum inhale to maximum exhale) [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why the spirometer trace slopes downwards over time when soda lime is used. (3)
questions.solution:
Oxygen is used in respiration [B1]
Exhaled CO₂ is absorbed by soda lime [B1]
So the total volume of gas in the chamber falls [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the roles of cartilage, smooth muscle, elastic fibres and ciliated epithelium in the airways. (3)
questions.solution:
Cartilage keeps the trachea / bronchi open [B1]
Smooth muscle can contract to narrow airways; elastic fibres recoil to help exhale [B1]
Ciliated epithelium and goblet cells trap and remove pathogens / dust in mucus [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the role of muscles in expiration at rest and during forced expiration. (1)
questions.solution: At rest it is passive (external intercostals and diaphragm relax; elastic recoil); forced expiration uses internal intercostal and abdominal muscle contraction [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the changes that cause air to enter the lungs during inspiration. (1)
questions.solution: Diaphragm contracts and flattens, external intercostals contract, ribs move up and out; thorax volume increases, pressure falls below atmospheric so air enters [B1]

questions.prompt: Give the function of the cartilage rings in the trachea. (1)
questions.solution: Keep the trachea open / prevent collapse when air pressure falls during inspiration [B1]

questions.prompt: Place myoglobin, fetal haemoglobin and adult haemoglobin in order of affinity for oxygen, highest first. (1)
hints: Fetal haemoglobin must take oxygen from the mother.
questions.solution: Myoglobin > fetal haemoglobin > adult haemoglobin [B1]

questions.prompt: Which way does the oxygen dissociation curve shift at high CO₂ concentration? (1)
questions.solution: To the right (lower affinity, more oxygen released) [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why the oxygen dissociation curve of haemoglobin is S-shaped. (1)
questions.solution: Binding of the first O₂ changes the shape of haemoglobin, making it easier for further O₂ molecules to bind (cooperative binding) [B1]

questions.prompt: Compare the pressure changes in the left ventricle and left atrium during one cardiac cycle. (4)
questions.solution:
Both rise and fall during the cycle [B1]
Ventricular pressure rises much higher (about 16 kPa) than atrial pressure (about 1–2 kPa) [B1]
Atrial pressure is higher than ventricular pressure during atrial systole / ventricular filling [B1]
Ventricular pressure rises sharply during ventricular systole while atrial pressure stays low [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the events of the cardiac cycle. (4)
questions.solution:
Atrial systole: atria contract, pushing blood into the ventricles through open AV valves [B1]
Ventricular systole: ventricles contract, AV valves close, pressure rises [B1]
Semilunar valves open and blood is forced into the aorta and pulmonary artery [B1]
Diastole: heart relaxes, semilunar valves close, blood fills atria and ventricles [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why the pressure in the aorta never falls to zero during the cardiac cycle. (4)
questions.solution:
Aorta walls contain elastic tissue [B1]
They stretch when blood is forced in during ventricular systole [B1]
Recoil during diastole, maintaining pressure [B1]
Semilunar valve closes, preventing backflow into the ventricle [B1]

questions.prompt:
One cardiac cycle on a pressure trace lasts 0.75 s, and aortic pressure ranges from 10.5 kPa to 16.0 kPa.

(i) Calculate the heart rate to 2 significant figures. (1)
(ii) Calculate the percentage increase from minimum to maximum aortic pressure, to 2 significant figures. (2)

(i) A pressure trace shows 3 complete cardiac cycles in 2.4 s. Calculate the heart rate. (2)
(ii) Name the valve that closes when ventricular pressure first exceeds atrial pressure. (1)
questions.solution:
(i) 2.4 ÷ 3 = 0.8 s per cycle [M1]
60 ÷ 0.8 = 75 bpm [A1]
(ii) Atrioventricular (bicuspid / mitral on the left) valve [B1]

questions.prompt:
A person's resting heart rate is 64 bpm and stroke volume is 75 cm³. During exercise, heart rate rises to 150 bpm and stroke volume to 120 cm³.

Calculate the percentage increase in cardiac output. (3)
Compare and contrast the circulatory systems of mammals and fish. (6)
questions.solution:
Both are closed systems with blood in vessels, pumped by a heart [B1]
Fish have a single circulation — blood passes through the heart once per circuit [B1]
Mammals have a double circulation — pulmonary and systemic [B1]
Fish heart has two chambers; mammal heart has four [B1]
In fish, blood pressure falls after the gills, so flow to body is slow [B1]
In mammals, blood returns to the heart to be repressurised, so high pressure to the body [B1]
Level-marked (5–6 marks).

questions.prompt: Compare open and closed circulatory systems, using insects and mammals as examples. (6)
questions.solution:
Insects have an open system; blood (haemolymph) is not always in vessels [B1]
Haemolymph bathes organs directly in the body cavity (haemocoel) [B1]
Pumped by a tube-like heart at low pressure [B1]
Mammals have a closed system — blood always in vessels [B1]
Higher pressure and faster flow, so substances delivered quickly [B1]
Insects don't carry oxygen in blood — tracheal system instead [B1]
Level-marked (5–6 marks).

questions.prompt: Explain why large, active animals need a specialised transport system. (6)
questions.solution:
Large animals have a small surface area to volume ratio [B1]
Diffusion distances to inner cells are too long [B1]
Active animals have a high metabolic rate, needing lots of oxygen and glucose [B1]
And produce lots of waste (CO₂, urea) [B1]
Mass transport moves substances quickly over long distances [B1]
Also transports hormones / heat / immune cells [B1]
Level-marked (5–6 marks).

questions.prompt:
Squid blood contains haemocyanin. At high CO₂ partial pressure, haemocyanin's affinity for oxygen falls.

Suggest a mechanism for this. (2)
questions.solution:
CO₂ forms carbonic acid, releasing H⁺ (lower pH) [B1]
H⁺ binds to / alters the tertiary structure of haemocyanin, reducing its affinity for O₂ [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how most carbon dioxide is transported in the blood. (2)
questions.solution:
CO₂ enters red blood cells and combines with water to form carbonic acid, catalysed by carbonic anhydrase [B1]
Dissociates into H⁺ and HCO₃⁻; HCO₃⁻ diffuses into plasma (chloride shift) [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain the role of haemoglobin as a buffer in red blood cells. (2)
questions.solution:
Haemoglobin accepts H⁺ ions released from carbonic acid, forming haemoglobinic acid [B1]
Prevents the pH of the blood falling / encourages oxygen release [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why the blood vessels visible under the skin of the arm are likely to be veins. (3)
questions.solution:
Veins are near the surface; arteries are deeper and protected [B1]
Veins have thin walls and wide lumens; blood is dark red (deoxygenated) [B1]
No pulse can be felt / blood flows towards the heart [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how blood is returned to the heart in the veins of the legs. (3)
questions.solution:
Valves prevent backflow [B1]
Contraction of skeletal muscles squeezes veins, pushing blood towards the heart [B1]
Breathing movements lower pressure in the thorax, helping return [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the structure of an arteriole and explain how it controls blood flow. (3)
questions.solution:
Arteriole wall has a high proportion of smooth muscle [B1]
Contraction narrows the lumen (vasoconstriction), reducing blood flow to capillaries [B1]
Relaxation widens it (vasodilation), increasing flow [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how ECG traces would differ for a person with tachycardia, bradycardia, and atrial fibrillation. (4)
questions.solution:
Tachycardia: heart rate above 100 bpm — waves closer together [B1]
Bradycardia: heart rate below 60 bpm — waves further apart [B1]
Atrial fibrillation: no clear P waves / irregular small waves [B1]
And irregular QRS complexes / irregular rhythm [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why very fit athletes often have a low resting heart rate. (4)
questions.solution:
Training makes cardiac muscle larger / stronger [B1]
So stroke volume increases [B1]
The same cardiac output can be maintained with fewer beats [B1]
Greater parasympathetic (vagal) activity [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe what each part of a normal ECG represents. (4)
questions.solution:
P wave — atrial depolarisation (atrial systole) [B1]
QRS complex — ventricular depolarisation (ventricular systole) [B1]
T wave — ventricular repolarisation (diastole) [B1]
PR interval — delay at the AVN [B1]

questions.prompt:
In week 20 of pregnancy, a woman's stroke volume was 80 cm³ and heart rate 85 bpm.

(i) Calculate her cardiac output, with units. (3)
(ii) Suggest one advantage of the increase in cardiac output in pregnancy. (1)
questions.solution:
(i) 80 × 85 [M1]
= 6800 [A1]
cm³ min⁻¹ (6.8 dm³ min⁻¹) [B1]
(ii) More oxygen and nutrients delivered to the placenta / fetus [B1]

questions.prompt: Cardiac output is 5.6 dm³ min⁻¹ and heart rate is 70 bpm. Calculate the stroke volume in cm³, and explain how stroke volume increases with training. (4)
questions.solution:
5600 ÷ 70 [M1]
= 80 cm³ [A1]
Training makes cardiac muscle larger / stronger [B1]
So the ventricles fill and empty more fully with each beat [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how heart rate is increased during exercise. (4)
questions.solution:
Chemoreceptors in the carotid / aortic bodies detect rising CO₂ / falling pH [B1]
Impulses sent to the cardiovascular centre in the medulla [B1]
More impulses along sympathetic nerves to the SAN [B1]
SAN fires more frequently; adrenaline also increases rate [B1]

questions.prompt:
During pregnancy, cardiac output rises by about 40 % while mean arterial blood pressure falls slightly. A student concluded that resistance in the blood vessels has decreased.

Evaluate this conclusion. (3)
questions.solution:
If more blood is pumped but pressure falls, resistance must fall — supports the conclusion [B1]
Likely due to vasodilation / growth of the placental circulation [B1]
But data are means / correlation; other factors (blood volume, hormones) could contribute [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why blood pressure falls as blood moves from arteries to capillaries to veins. (3)
questions.solution:
Further from the heart, so less pressure from ventricular contraction [B1]
Arterioles and capillaries have a huge total cross-sectional area [B1]
Friction / resistance and loss of fluid as tissue fluid reduce pressure [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how vasoconstriction of arterioles affects blood pressure and blood flow to tissues. (3)
questions.solution:
Smooth muscle in arteriole walls contracts, narrowing the lumen [B1]
Increases resistance, so blood pressure rises upstream [B1]
Less blood flows to the tissues supplied by those arterioles [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe blood flow through the left side of the heart during the cardiac cycle, and explain the roles of the valves and pressure differences. (6)
questions.solution:
Oxygenated blood enters the left atrium from the pulmonary vein [B1]
Atrial pressure exceeds ventricular, so the bicuspid (mitral) valve opens; atrial systole pushes blood into the ventricle [B1]
Ventricular systole raises pressure above atrial pressure, closing the bicuspid valve to prevent backflow [B1]
When ventricular pressure exceeds aortic pressure, the semilunar valve opens and blood enters the aorta [B1]
In diastole, ventricular pressure falls below aortic pressure, closing the semilunar valve [B1]
Chordae tendineae stop the AV valve turning inside out; blood flows in one direction only [B1]
Level-marked (5–6 marks).

questions.prompt: Describe the structure of the human heart and explain how it is adapted for its function. (6)
questions.solution:
Four chambers — two atria and two ventricles [B1]
Septum separates oxygenated and deoxygenated blood [B1]
Left ventricle wall is thickest, generating high pressure for systemic circulation [B1]
Atria have thin walls — only pump into the ventricles [B1]
AV and semilunar valves prevent backflow [B1]
Coronary arteries supply cardiac muscle with oxygen; muscle is myogenic [B1]
Level-marked (5–6 marks).

questions.prompt: Explain how heart action is initiated and coordinated. (6)
questions.solution:
Cardiac muscle is myogenic — contracts without nervous stimulation [B1]
SAN generates waves of excitation, spreading across the atria, which contract [B1]
Non-conducting tissue prevents direct spread to ventricles [B1]
AVN delays the impulse, allowing atria to empty [B1]
Impulse passes down the bundle of His and Purkyne fibres to the apex [B1]
Ventricles contract from the apex upwards, pushing blood into arteries [B1]
Level-marked (5–6 marks).

questions.prompt:
(i) Describe where the oxygen dissociation curve of fetal haemoglobin lies relative to maternal haemoglobin. (1)
(ii) Explain how the different affinities allow oxygen transfer to the fetus. (3)
questions.solution:
(i) To the left of the maternal curve [B1]
(ii) Fetal haemoglobin has a higher affinity for oxygen [B1]
At the low pO₂ in the placenta, maternal haemoglobin releases oxygen [B1]
Fetal haemoglobin picks it up / becomes more saturated at the same pO₂ [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how carbon monoxide poisoning reduces oxygen delivery to tissues. (4)
questions.solution:
CO binds to haem in haemoglobin [B1]
With a much higher affinity than oxygen / almost irreversibly [B1]
Forms carboxyhaemoglobin, so fewer sites for O₂ [B1]
Less oxygen carried and delivered; tissues respire anaerobically [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why a small fall in pO₂ in respiring tissues causes a large release of oxygen from haemoglobin. (4)
questions.solution:
The steep part of the sigmoid curve corresponds to the pO₂ in tissues [B1]
Small decrease in pO₂ causes large drop in saturation [B1]
Due to cooperative binding — as one O₂ leaves, the shape changes so others leave more easily [B1]
Bohr effect from CO₂ increases unloading further [B1]

questions.prompt: Plan an investigation to compare the rate of transpiration of two plant species using a potometer. (6)
questions.solution:
Use shoots of similar size from each species, cut under water [B1]
Keep light, temperature, humidity and air movement constant [B1]
Allow the shoot to acclimatise before recording [B1]
Measure the distance moved by the bubble in a set time; repeat several times [B1]
Calculate volume (πr²l) and divide by leaf surface area (trace leaves on graph paper) [B1]
Compare means statistically (t-test) [B1]
Level-marked (5–6 marks).

questions.prompt: Explain why a potometer measures water uptake rather than transpiration, and how to make the result closer to transpiration. (6)
questions.solution:
Potometer measures water taken up by the shoot [B1]
Some water is used in photosynthesis / for turgor [B1]
But about 99 % of water taken up is transpired, so uptake is a good estimate [B1]
Accurate results need an airtight seal and no air in the xylem [B1]
Measure mass loss of a whole potted plant (with soil covered) as an alternative [B1]
Express per unit leaf area for comparison [B1]
Level-marked (5–6 marks).

questions.prompt: Plan an investigation to compare the stomatal density of the upper and lower surfaces of a leaf. (6)
questions.solution:
Paint clear nail varnish on each surface and allow to dry [B1]
Peel off with sticky tape and mount on a slide [B1]
Count stomata in a field of view at high power [B1]
Calculate the area of the field of view using a stage micrometer (πr²) [B1]
Repeat in several fields / leaves and calculate the mean density per mm² [B1]
Compare surfaces using a t-test [B1]
Level-marked (5–6 marks).

questions.prompt: Explain, with examples of transported substances, why multicellular plants need transport systems. (3)
questions.solution:
Large plants have a small surface area to volume ratio, so diffusion is too slow [B1]
