Water and mineral ions must be moved from roots to leaves [B1]
Sugars (sucrose) / amino acids must be moved from leaves to other parts (roots, fruits) [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the distribution of xylem and phloem in a root, stem and leaf of a dicotyledonous plant. (3)
questions.solution:
Root: central vascular cylinder with xylem in an X shape, phloem between the arms [B1]
Stem: vascular bundles around the edge, xylem inside, phloem outside [B1]
Leaf: vascular bundles in veins / midrib, xylem above phloem [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why the arrangement of vascular tissue in a root helps it resist pulling forces, while in a stem it resists bending. (3)
questions.solution:
Root: central xylem acts like a cable, resisting pulling / tension as the plant moves [B1]
Stem: bundles around the outside give support / scaffolding [B1]
Resists bending in wind [B1]

questions.prompt: Give three functions of a vascular bundle (vein) in a leaf. (3)
questions.solution:
Xylem brings water and mineral ions to the leaf [B1]
Phloem transports sucrose away from the leaf [B1]
Provides support for the leaf [B1]

questions.prompt: Name three tissues seen in a transverse section of a leaf and give the function of each. (3)
questions.solution:
Palisade mesophyll — main site of photosynthesis [B1]
Spongy mesophyll — air spaces for gas exchange [B1]
Epidermis / guard cells / cuticle — protection and control of water loss / gas exchange [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how the palisade mesophyll is adapted for photosynthesis. (3)
questions.solution:
Near the upper surface where light is brightest [B1]
Tall, column-shaped cells packed closely [B1]
Many chloroplasts that can move towards light [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how the structure of xylem vessels is adapted to their function. (4)
questions.solution:
Dead, with no cytoplasm or end walls, so a continuous tube with little resistance [B1]
Lignin strengthens walls, preventing collapse under tension [B1]
Lignin waterproofs the walls [B1]
Pits allow water to move sideways between vessels [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how the structure of phloem is adapted to its function. (4)
questions.solution:
Sieve tube elements have few organelles, so less resistance to flow [B1]
Sieve plates with pores join elements end to end [B1]
Companion cells have many mitochondria for active loading of sucrose [B1]
Plasmodesmata link companion cells and sieve tubes [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the mass flow hypothesis for translocation in phloem. (4)
questions.solution:
Sucrose actively loaded into sieve tubes at the source (via companion cells, H⁺ co-transport) [B1]
Lowers water potential, so water enters from xylem by osmosis [B1]
Hydrostatic pressure rises at the source [B1]
At the sink sucrose is removed, water leaves; pressure gradient drives mass flow from source to sink [B1]

questions.prompt:
Mutant barley without root hairs grew less and took up less phosphate than normal barley. When grown with mycorrhizal fungi, the mutants grew almost as well as normal plants.

Evaluate the conclusion that the mycorrhiza compensated for the lack of root hairs. (3)
questions.solution:
Mutants with mycorrhiza had similar dry mass / phosphate to normal plants — supports the conclusion [B1]
Mycorrhizal hyphae increase the surface area for absorbing phosphate [B1]
But no statistical test / repeats / SD given; the fungus might also affect normal plants [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the pathways water takes across the root to the xylem. (3)
questions.solution:
Apoplast pathway through cell walls [B1]
Symplast pathway through cytoplasm and plasmodesmata [B1]
At the endodermis, the Casparian strip blocks the apoplast, so water must enter the symplast [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how root pressure is generated. (3)
questions.solution:
Endodermis cells actively transport mineral ions into the xylem [B1]
Lowering the water potential in the xylem [B1]
Water moves in by osmosis, pushing water up the xylem [B1]

questions.prompt:
(i) Describe what is meant by the transpiration stream. (2)
(ii) Scientists injected dye into a borehole in a tree trunk and then sealed it with tape. Suggest why. (1)
(iii) Suggest how a student could observe the route of water in a sunflower stem using food dye. (2)
questions.solution:
(i) Movement of water from roots to leaves through the xylem [B1]
Driven by evaporation of water from leaves (transpiration) and cohesion–tension [B1]
(ii) To stop air entering the xylem / prevent dye leaking / stop the hole drying out [B1]
(iii) Stand cut stem in dye solution for some time [B1]
Cut thin cross-sections at intervals and view under a microscope to see stained xylem [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how water moves up the xylem by the cohesion–tension mechanism. (5)
questions.solution:
Water evaporates from mesophyll cells and diffuses out through stomata [B1]
Water moves from the xylem to replace it [B1]
Creates tension (negative pressure) in the xylem [B1]
Water molecules are cohesive (hydrogen bonds), so a continuous column is pulled up [B1]
Adhesion to xylem walls also helps [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how to use a potometer to measure the rate of water uptake by a shoot. (5)
questions.solution:
Cut the shoot underwater at a slant to prevent air entering the xylem [B1]
Assemble the potometer underwater; seal joints with petroleum jelly [B1]
Dry the leaves; allow the shoot to acclimatise [B1]
Introduce an air bubble and measure distance moved in a set time [B1]
Calculate volume = πr² × distance; reset with the reservoir and repeat [B1]

questions.prompt:
(i) Explain why plants wilted after being watered with a fertiliser solution 1000 times too concentrated. (3)
(ii) Cyanide inhibits ATP synthesis. Assess whether it would cause the same wilting effect. (2)
(iii) Explain why plants in bright light need more water than shaded plants at the same temperature. (2)
questions.solution:
(i) Soil water potential became lower than that of root hair cells [B1]
Water moved out of roots by osmosis / no water uptake [B1]
Cells lost turgor, so the plant wilted [B1]
(ii) Partly — cyanide stops active transport of minerals, so less root pressure / less water uptake [B1]
But transpiration pull is passive, so water still moves; wilting would be less / different cause [B1]
(iii) More stomata open in bright light for CO₂ uptake [B1]
So more water lost by transpiration [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how each of these affects the rate of transpiration: light intensity, temperature, humidity, air movement. (7)
questions.solution:
Light: stomata open in light, increasing transpiration [B1]
Temperature: water molecules have more kinetic energy, so evaporation and diffusion are faster [B1]

Maintaining a steep water potential gradient, so transpiration increases [B1]
Rate depends on whichever factor is limiting [B1]

questions.prompt: Compare the adaptations of xerophytes and hydrophytes. (7)
questions.solution:
Xerophytes live in dry conditions and reduce water loss [B1]
Thick waxy cuticle, sunken stomata, hairs, rolled leaves [B1]
Reduced leaves (spines), deep / widespread roots, water storage tissue [B1]
Hydrophytes live in water [B1]
Stomata on the upper surface of floating leaves [B1]
Large air spaces (aerenchyma) for buoyancy and oxygen supply [B1]
Thin / no cuticle, little lignified xylem [B1]

questions.prompt: Give one way that new medicines are being developed. (1)
questions.solution: Computer modelling of drug–receptor shapes / screening natural sources (plants, microorganisms) / GM bacteria producing drugs [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why it is important to conserve biodiversity for the development of new medicines. (1)
questions.solution: Many medicines come from organisms, and undiscovered species may produce useful compounds [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain what is meant by personalised medicine. (1)
questions.solution: Treatment chosen based on a person's genetic information, so drugs are more effective / fewer side effects [B1]

questions.prompt: Name two types of cell that are produced during the primary immune response. (1)
questions.solution: Plasma cells and memory cells [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the cells that release histamine during inflammation. (1)
questions.solution: Mast cells [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how platelets help to prevent infection after a cut. (1)
questions.solution: They start the clotting cascade, forming a clot that seals the wound and stops pathogens entering [B1]

questions.prompt: Give two ways of reducing the spread of a disease transmitted by droplets. (1)
questions.solution: Reduce overcrowding (fewer people per house) and improve ventilation / cover coughs [B1]

questions.prompt: Give two ways a fungal tree disease could spread between countries. (1)
questions.solution: Spores carried on the wind and import of infected young trees / soil [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the polysaccharide plants produce to block sieve plates and plasmodesmata when attacked by pathogens. (1)
questions.solution: Callose [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the type of pathogen that causes ring rot in potatoes. (1)
questions.solution: Bacterium [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the type of pathogen that causes ringworm. (1)
questions.solution: Fungus [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the type of pathogen that causes potato late blight. (1)
questions.solution: Protoctist (Phytophthora) [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how mucous membranes make it harder for influenza virus to enter the body. (2)
questions.solution:
Mucus traps pathogens [B1]
Cilia waft mucus to the throat to be swallowed; mucus contains lysozyme / phagocytes [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how the skin acts as a barrier to pathogens. (2)
questions.solution:
Outer layer of dead keratinised cells is a physical barrier [B1]
Sebum is acidic / contains antimicrobial chemicals; skin flora outcompete pathogens [B1]

questions.prompt: Give two other primary non-specific defences of the body. (2)
questions.solution:
Stomach acid kills pathogens [B1]
Lysozyme in tears / blood clotting seals wounds / expulsive reflexes (coughing, sneezing) [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the sequence of events in the primary immune response, from antigen presentation to memory cell formation. (5)
hints: APC, T helper, clonal selection, expansion.
questions.solution:
Antigen presentation by macrophages (APCs) [B1]
T helper cells with complementary receptors bind and are activated; release interleukins [B1]
Clonal selection — B cells with complementary antibodies are selected [B1]
Clonal expansion — selected B cells divide by mitosis [B1]
Differentiate into plasma cells (antibodies) and memory cells [B1]

questions.prompt: Compare the primary and secondary immune responses. (5)
questions.solution:
Primary response is slower — lag of several days [B1]
Lower antibody concentration [B1]
Secondary response is faster and larger [B1]
Because memory cells already exist [B1]
Pathogen destroyed before symptoms appear; antibodies remain longer [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the roles of the different types of T lymphocyte. (5)
questions.solution:
T helper cells release interleukins that stimulate B cells and phagocytes [B1]
T killer cells attach to infected cells and release perforin, killing them [B1]
T regulatory cells suppress the immune response once the pathogen is gone [B1]
Prevent autoimmunity [B1]
T memory cells give rapid response on reinfection [B1]

questions.prompt:
Snakebite antivenom contains Fab fragments — the antigen-binding arms of sheep antibodies, without the constant region.

(i) Name the type of immunity given. (1)
(ii) Give two similarities and one difference between a Fab fragment and a whole antibody. (3)
questions.solution:
(i) Artificial passive immunity [B1]
(ii) Similarity: both have variable regions / antigen-binding sites [B1]
Similarity: both contain heavy and light chains held by disulfide bridges [B1]
Difference: Fab has one binding site / no constant region / no hinge [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe four ways in which antibodies help destroy pathogens. (4)
questions.solution:
Act as opsonins, marking pathogens for phagocytosis [B1]
Agglutination — clumping pathogens together [B1]
Neutralise toxins (antitoxins) [B1]
Block binding sites so pathogens can't enter cells [B1]

questions.prompt: Give an example of each type of immunity: natural active, artificial active, natural passive, artificial passive. (4)
questions.solution:
Natural active — recovering from an infection [B1]
Artificial active — vaccination [B1]
Natural passive — antibodies across the placenta / in breast milk [B1]
Artificial passive — injection of antibodies (e.g. tetanus antitoxin) [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why many pathogenic bacteria are now resistant to several antibiotics. (3)
questions.solution:
Random mutations produce resistance alleles [B1]
Overuse / misuse of antibiotics selects for resistant bacteria, which survive and reproduce [B1]
Resistance genes on plasmids are passed between bacteria (horizontal transfer), combining resistances [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest three ways to reduce the development of antibiotic resistance. (3)
questions.solution:
Only prescribe antibiotics when needed (not for viral infections) [B1]
Patients complete the full course [B1]
Reduce use in farming / improve hospital hygiene / rotate antibiotics [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why patients in hospital are more at risk of infection by MRSA. (3)
questions.solution:
Many patients have weakened immune systems / open wounds [B1]
Heavy antibiotic use selects for resistant strains [B1]
Close contact with staff and patients spreads bacteria [B1]

questions.prompt: Outline how synthetic biology can help provide new medicines. (2)
questions.solution:
Designing and building new biological systems / modifying organisms [B1]
e.g. engineered bacteria or yeast produce drugs (insulin, artemisinin) / design new antibiotics [B1]

questions.prompt: Give two sources of new medicines. (2)
questions.solution:
Plants / microorganisms / animals (e.g. penicillin from fungi, aspirin from willow) [B1]
Computer modelling of target molecules / personalised medicine [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how pharmacogenomics could improve treatment of disease. (2)
questions.solution:
Genetic differences affect how people respond to drugs [B1]
Knowing a patient's genotype allows the best drug and dose to be chosen, with fewer side effects [B1]

questions.prompt:
Which of these is most likely to increase biodiversity?

Choose one answer.

A  Captive breeding programmes
B  Climate change
C  Human population growth
D  Monoculture farming (1)
hints: The others reduce habitats or species.
questions.solution: A — captive breeding programmes. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how monoculture reduces biodiversity. (1)
hints: One crop over a large area.
questions.solution: Only one species grown, with hedgerows removed and pesticides / herbicides killing other species, so fewer habitats and species [B1]

questions.prompt: Give one way in which agricultural land can be managed to increase biodiversity. (1)
questions.solution: Planting hedgerows / leaving wildflower field margins / crop rotation / reducing pesticide use [B1]

questions.prompt:
In a coppiced area, a survey found 12 bluebells, 8 primroses, 6 wood anemones and 4 violets.

Calculate Simpson's Index of Diversity, D = 1 − Σ(n/N)². (3)
Two habitats have Simpson's index values of 0.49 and 0.71. Explain what these values show. (3)
questions.solution:
Simpson's index ranges from 0 to 1 [B1]
Higher value shows greater biodiversity [B1]
So the 0.71 habitat has more species and / or a more even spread of individuals [B1]

questions.prompt: A habitat contains 50 individuals of species A and nothing else. Calculate Simpson's Index of Diversity and explain the result. (3)
questions.solution:
Σ(n/N)² = 1² = 1 [M1]
D = 1 − 1 = 0 [A1]
Zero diversity — only one species present [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how biodiversity can be considered at three different levels. (3)
questions.solution:
Habitat diversity — the number of different habitats in an area [B1]
Species diversity — species richness and evenness [B1]
Genetic diversity — the variety of alleles within a species [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how to calculate genetic diversity using the proportion of polymorphic gene loci. (3)
questions.solution:
A polymorphic locus has two or more alleles [B1]
Proportion = number of polymorphic loci ÷ total number of loci [B1]
Higher proportion = greater genetic diversity [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why species evenness is important when comparing biodiversity. (3)
hints: Two communities with the same richness.
questions.solution:
Evenness is how close in numbers each species is [B1]
A community with even numbers is more stable / diverse than one dominated by one species [B1]
Two habitats with the same richness can have very different biodiversity [B1]

questions.prompt: An ancient woodland has a Simpson's Index of Diversity of 0.85. What does this show? (1)
questions.solution: High biodiversity — many species with fairly even numbers [B1]

questions.prompt: What would a Simpson's Index of Diversity of 0.1 suggest about a habitat? (1)
questions.solution: Low biodiversity — few species / dominated by one species [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why a high Simpson's index is linked to a stable ecosystem. (1)
questions.solution: Many species with complex food webs, so the loss of one species has less effect [B1]

questions.prompt: Give one ecological, one economic and one aesthetic reason for maintaining biodiversity. (3)
questions.solution:
Ecological: keystone species / food webs / herbivores are food for predators / prevents soil erosion [B1]
Economic: tourism / sustainable hunting / new medicines / crop genes [B1]
Aesthetic: enjoyment of landscapes and wildlife / mental wellbeing [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why maintaining genetic diversity in wild relatives of crop plants is important. (3)
questions.solution:
Wild relatives contain alleles not found in crop varieties [B1]
e.g. for disease resistance, drought tolerance [B1]
These alleles can be bred into crops to adapt to future challenges [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how loss of biodiversity can affect the stability of an ecosystem. (3)
questions.solution:
Fewer species mean simpler food webs [B1]
Loss of one species has a greater effect on others [B1]
Less able to resist / recover from disturbance (e.g. disease, climate change) [B1]

questions.prompt:
Mean number per quadrat: grass 26, daisy 7, clover 6, plantain 4, dandelion 4, buttercup 2, moss 1.

(i) Calculate Simpson's Index of Diversity, D = 1 − Σ(n/N)². (3)
(ii) Explain how grouping all grass species as "grass" affects D. (2)
questions.solution:
(i) N = 50 [M1]
Σ(n/N)² = 0.2704 + 0.0196 + 0.0144 + 0.0064 + 0.0064 + 0.0016 + 0.0004 = 0.319 [M1]
D = 0.681 [A1]
(ii) Several grass species counted as one, so species richness is underestimated [B1]
And one 'species' appears dominant, so D is lower than the true value [B1]

questions.prompt:
Habitat X: 10 of species A, 10 of B, 10 of C. Habitat Y: 28 of A, 1 of B, 1 of C.

Calculate D for each and explain the difference. (5)
questions.solution:
X: Σ(n/N)² = 3 × (1/3)² = 0.333; D = 0.667 [M1 A1]
Y: (28/30)² + 2 × (1/30)² = 0.871 + 0.002 = 0.873; D = 0.127 [M1 A1]
Same richness, but X is more even so has higher diversity [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why identifying species accurately matters when calculating Simpson's index, and how students can ensure accuracy. (5)
questions.solution:
Misidentifying species changes species richness [B1]
And changes the numbers of each species, affecting evenness [B1]
So D would be inaccurate [B1]
Use identification keys / guides [B1]
Check with an expert / photograph uncertain specimens [B1]

questions.prompt: Give one problem associated with artificial selection in farm animals. (1)
questions.solution: Inbreeding / reduced genetic diversity / increased frequency of harmful recessive alleles / health problems [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how artificial selection could be used to produce cows with a high milk yield. (1)
questions.solution: Select cows with the highest milk yield (and bulls from such mothers), breed them, and repeat over many generations [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why gene banks of wild varieties are important. (1)
questions.solution: They preserve alleles lost through selective breeding, which may be needed in future (e.g. disease resistance) [B1]

questions.prompt: Name a molecule commonly compared between species to work out evolutionary relationships. (1)
questions.solution: Cytochrome c / rRNA / DNA [B1]

questions.prompt: Distinguish between intraspecific and interspecific competition. (1)
questions.solution: Intraspecific: between members of the same species; interspecific: between different species for the same resources [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why more differences in DNA base sequence suggest two species are less closely related. (1)
questions.solution: Mutations accumulate over time, so more differences mean longer since they shared a common ancestor [B1]

questions.prompt: Correct the errors in this summary: "Baroreceptors detect falls in blood pH and send impulses to the cerebellum. More impulses along the vagus nerve speed up the heart. Adrenaline decreases the force of contraction." (4)
questions.solution:
Chemoreceptors (not baroreceptors) detect changes in blood pH / CO₂ [B1]
Impulses go to the medulla oblongata (not the cerebellum) [B1]
The vagus (parasympathetic) nerve slows the heart; sympathetic nerves speed it up [B1]
Adrenaline increases the force of contraction and heart rate [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how baroreceptors help control blood pressure. (4)
questions.solution:
Baroreceptors in the aorta and carotid arteries detect stretching of the walls [B1]
High pressure — more impulses to the medulla [B1]
Medulla sends impulses along parasympathetic nerves, reducing heart rate [B1]
Low pressure — sympathetic impulses increase heart rate [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the organisation of the human nervous system. (4)
questions.solution:
Central nervous system — brain and spinal cord [B1]
Peripheral nervous system — all other neurones [B1]
PNS split into somatic (voluntary) and autonomic (involuntary) [B1]
Autonomic split into sympathetic and parasympathetic [B1]

questions.prompt: Give the meaning of cell signalling. (1)
questions.solution: Communication between cells using chemical messengers (e.g. hormones, neurotransmitters, cytokines) that bind to receptors on target cells [B1]

questions.prompt:
Which of these is not an example of cell signalling?

Choose one answer.

A  Acetylcholine binding to receptors on a muscle
B  Insulin binding to a liver cell receptor
C  Glucose being filtered out of the blood in the glomerulus
D  T helper cells releasing cytokines (1)
hints: Which one involves a chemical messenger binding to a receptor?
questions.solution: C — glucose being filtered in the glomerulus. [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why a hormone only affects its target cells. (1)
questions.solution: Only target cells have receptors with a shape complementary to the hormone [B1]

questions.prompt: Acetylcholine is made in a squid's nervous system but can affect its skin cells. Explain how. (2)
questions.solution:
Acetylcholine is released from nerve endings near skin cells / diffuses or travels to them [B1]
Binds to complementary receptors on skin cells, causing a response (e.g. colour change) [B1]

questions.prompt: Compare nervous and hormonal communication. (2)
questions.solution:
Nervous: electrical impulses along neurones, fast, short-lived, localised [B1]
Hormonal: chemicals in the blood, slower, longer-lasting, widespread [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain what is meant by a second messenger, using adrenaline as an example. (2)
questions.solution:
Adrenaline (first messenger) binds to a membrane receptor but doesn't enter the cell [B1]
Activates adenylyl cyclase, producing cAMP (second messenger) inside the cell, which triggers the response [B1]

questions.prompt: Give the meaning of homeostasis. (1)
questions.solution: Maintaining a constant internal environment within narrow limits despite external changes [B1]

questions.prompt: Give one example of positive feedback in the body. (1)
questions.solution: Oxytocin release during childbirth / blood clotting / depolarisation in an action potential [B1]

questions.prompt: Compare ectotherms and endotherms. (1)
questions.solution: Ectotherms rely mainly on external heat sources and behaviour; endotherms generate heat internally and use physiological responses [B1]

questions.prompt:
(i) Define endotherm. (1)
(ii) Give one advantage and one disadvantage of being an ectotherm. (2)
questions.solution:
(i) An animal that maintains its body temperature mainly using heat from metabolic reactions [B1]
(ii) Advantage: needs less food as less energy used to generate heat [B1]
Disadvantage: less active in cold conditions / more vulnerable to predators [B1]

questions.prompt: Give one advantage and two disadvantages of being an endotherm. (3)
questions.solution:
Advantage: can be active at any temperature / colonise cold habitats [B1]
Disadvantage: needs much more food for respiration [B1]
Disadvantage: risk of overheating in hot climates [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe three physiological responses of an endotherm to a fall in environmental temperature. (3)
questions.solution:
Vasoconstriction of arterioles in the skin [B1]
Shivering [B1]
Hair erection / reduced sweating / increased metabolic rate (thyroxine) [B1]

questions.prompt: Discuss two statements: (1) ectotherms cannot control their body temperature; (2) only ectotherms use behavioural responses to control temperature. (6)
questions.solution:
Statement 1 is wrong — ectotherms control temperature by behaviour [B1]
e.g. lizards bask in the sun / orientate body to the sun [B1]
e.g. move to shade / burrows; some can change heart rate / colour [B1]
Statement 2 is wrong — endotherms also use behaviour [B1]
e.g. humans wear clothes, seek shade; dogs pant; elephants flap ears [B1]
Animals huddle / hibernate / migrate [B1]
Level-marked (5–6 marks).

questions.prompt: Explain how the body responds to a rise in core temperature. (6)
questions.solution:
Thermoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect the rise [B1]
Sweat glands secrete more sweat — evaporation cools [B1]
Arterioles in skin dilate — more heat lost by radiation [B1]
Hairs lie flat — less insulation [B1]
Metabolic rate reduced [B1]
Negative feedback restores the set point [B1]
Level-marked (5–6 marks).

questions.prompt: Explain how negative feedback maintains blood glucose concentration. (6)
questions.solution:
Rise in blood glucose detected by β cells; insulin released [B1]
Insulin increases glucose uptake and glycogenesis [B1]
Blood glucose falls back to normal [B1]
Fall in blood glucose detected by α cells; glucagon released [B1]
Glucagon stimulates glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis in the liver [B1]
Blood glucose rises back to normal — response reverses the change [B1]
Level-marked (5–6 marks).

questions.prompt:
During infection, pyrogens cause prostaglandin E₂ (PGE₂) to bind to receptors in the hypothalamus, raising the temperature set point.

(ii) State two functions of cell surface membranes shown by PGE₂ binding to receptors. (2)
questions.solution:

Body temperature rises (fever), which may slow pathogen growth / speed immune responses [B1]

Partially permeable barrier / triggers a response inside the cell / cell recognition [B1]

questions.prompt: Aspirin inhibits the enzyme COX-2, which makes PGE₂. Explain how aspirin reduces fever. (4)
questions.solution:
Aspirin inhibits COX-2 [B1]
So less PGE₂ is made [B1]
Less PGE₂ binds to receptors in the hypothalamus [B1]
Set point returns to normal, so temperature falls (sweating, vasodilation) [B1]

questions.prompt: Give four functions of membranes within cells. (4)
questions.solution:
Separate the cell into compartments with different conditions [B1]
Provide a surface for reactions, e.g. respiration on cristae / photosynthesis on thylakoids [B1]
Control what enters organelles (e.g. nuclear envelope pores) [B1]
Form vesicles for transport / isolate harmful enzymes (lysosomes) [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why damage to the hypothalamus can cause a person to produce large volumes of dilute urine. (1)
questions.solution: Less ADH is produced / released, so fewer aquaporins in collecting ducts and less water reabsorbed [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the gland that releases ADH into the blood. (1)
questions.solution: Posterior pituitary gland [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the channel proteins that ADH causes to be inserted in collecting duct cell membranes. (1)
questions.solution: Aquaporins [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why too much aldosterone can cause high blood pressure. (1)
questions.solution: More Na⁺ reabsorbed in the distal tubule / collecting duct, so more water follows by osmosis, increasing blood volume and pressure [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the part of the adrenal gland that secretes aldosterone. (1)
questions.solution: Adrenal cortex [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the part of the adrenal gland that secretes adrenaline. (1)
questions.solution: Adrenal medulla [B1]

questions.prompt:
Patient A: eGFR 160 cm³ min⁻¹, no protein in urine. Patient B: eGFR 45 cm³ min⁻¹, protein in urine and raised blood potassium. Normal eGFR is about 107 cm³ min⁻¹, and pregnancy can raise eGFR by 50–85 %.

Explain why the doctor concluded that A had a normal pregnancy and B had kidney failure. (4)
hints: Protein in urine means damaged glomeruli.
questions.solution:

A: no protein in urine — glomeruli intact [B1]
B: eGFR much lower than normal — kidneys filter poorly [B1]
B: protein in urine shows damaged filtration barrier; potassium not excreted so builds up in blood [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how haemodialysis treats kidney failure. (4)
questions.solution:
Blood passes through a dialyser with a partially permeable membrane [B1]
Dialysis fluid flows the other way (countercurrent), maintaining gradients [B1]
Urea and excess ions diffuse out of the blood [B1]
Dialysis fluid has the right concentration of glucose and ions, so useful substances are kept [B1]

questions.prompt: Compare kidney transplants with dialysis as treatments for kidney failure. (4)
questions.solution:
Transplant: patient free from regular dialysis sessions; better quality of life [B1]
Transplant: risk of rejection; immunosuppressant drugs for life increase infection risk [B1]
Dialysis: available without waiting for a donor [B1]
Dialysis: time-consuming, diet restrictions; long-term cheaper option is transplant [B1]

questions.prompt:
(i) Explain why ammonia is converted into urea in mammals. (1)
(ii) Name the process that removes the amine group from excess amino acids. (1)
questions.solution:
(i) Ammonia is very toxic and very soluble; urea is less toxic [B1]
(ii) Deamination [B1]

questions.prompt: Name two organs involved in excretion and the substance each excretes. (2)
questions.solution:
Lungs — carbon dioxide; kidneys — urea / water / salts [B1]
Liver — bile pigments; skin — sweat (urea, salts) [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the ornithine cycle. (2)
questions.solution:
Ammonia combines with CO₂ and ornithine to form citrulline, then arginine [B1]
Arginine is broken down to urea and ornithine, which is reused [B1]

questions.prompt:
(i) Name the three main regions of a kidney seen in a longitudinal section. (3)
(ii) A photomicrograph shows many glomeruli and convoluted tubules. Identify which region it is from and give a reason. (2)
questions.solution:
(i) Cortex [B1]
Medulla [B1]
Pelvis [B1]
(ii) Cortex [B1]
Glomeruli and convoluted tubules are found in the cortex [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the structure of the liver and its blood supply. (5)
questions.solution:
Hepatic artery brings oxygenated blood [B1]
Hepatic portal vein brings blood rich in absorbed nutrients from the gut [B1]
Blood mixes in sinusoids lined with hepatocytes [B1]
Kupffer cells in sinusoids remove old red blood cells [B1]
Blood leaves via the hepatic vein; bile made in hepatocytes drains to bile ducts [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe five functions of the liver. (5)
questions.solution:
Deamination of amino acids and urea formation [B1]
Detoxification of alcohol (ethanol → ethanal → acetate) and drugs [B1]
Storing glycogen and controlling blood glucose [B1]
Making bile / breaking down haemoglobin [B1]
Making plasma proteins / cholesterol; storing vitamins [B1]

questions.prompt:
(i) Name the part of the nephron where blood is at the highest hydrostatic pressure, and the part where ADH acts. (3)
(ii) Outline how the loop of Henle increases solute concentration in the medulla. (3)
questions.solution:
(i) Highest pressure: glomerulus (afferent arteriole wider than efferent) [B1]
ADH acts on the collecting duct (and distal convoluted tubule) [B1]
Mineral ions reabsorbed actively in the PCT / ascending limb [B1]

Water leaves the descending limb by osmosis, so filtrate becomes concentrated at the bottom [B1]
Countercurrent multiplier builds up a high solute concentration deep in the medulla [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe ultrafiltration and selective reabsorption in the nephron. (6)
questions.solution:
Afferent arteriole wider than efferent, giving high hydrostatic pressure in the glomerulus [B1]
Small molecules pass through the endothelium, basement membrane and podocytes [B1]
Blood cells and large proteins stay in the blood [B1]
In the PCT, Na⁺ actively pumped out of cells into blood [B1]
Glucose and amino acids co-transported with Na⁺ into PCT cells [B1]
Water follows by osmosis; microvilli and many mitochondria aid reabsorption [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how the body produces a small volume of concentrated urine after heavy sweating. (6)
questions.solution:
Sweating lowers the water potential of the blood [B1]
Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus shrink and are stimulated [B1]
Posterior pituitary releases more ADH [B1]
ADH binds to receptors on collecting duct cells, triggering cAMP [B1]
Vesicles with aquaporins fuse with the membrane [B1]
More water reabsorbed by osmosis into the medulla — less, concentrated urine [B1]

questions.prompt: A person lost 1 kg of fat over several weeks of dieting. Suggest what happened to the mass. (2)
questions.solution:
Fat was respired to provide energy [B1]
Mostly lost as CO₂ breathed out, and as water (breath, sweat, urine) [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how a urine test can detect pregnancy. (2)
questions.solution:
Pregnant women produce hCG, which is small enough to enter the urine [B1]
Monoclonal antibodies on the test stick bind hCG and give a coloured line [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how urine tests can detect anabolic steroids. (2)
questions.solution:
Steroids are small enough to be filtered into the urine [B1]
Detected by gas chromatography / mass spectrometry [B1]

questions.prompt:
Tetrodotoxin (TTX) binds to voltage-gated sodium channels and stops them opening.

(ii) Explain how paralysis of the diaphragm could lead to suffocation. (2)
questions.solution:
