Membrane can't depolarise / threshold not reached [B1]
No action potentials generated or propagated [B1]
No neurotransmitter released at synapses / neuromuscular junctions [B1]
(ii) Diaphragm can't contract, so thorax volume can't increase / air can't be drawn into lungs [B1]
No ventilation, so no oxygen reaches alveoli / CO₂ builds up [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how nicotine and curare have opposite effects at cholinergic synapses. (6)
questions.solution:
Nicotine has a similar shape to acetylcholine [B1]
Binds to ACh receptors and opens Na⁺ channels [B1]
Causes depolarisation / stimulates the postsynaptic membrane [B1]
Curare also binds to ACh receptors [B1]
But does not open Na⁺ channels — blocks ACh binding [B1]
So muscles are not stimulated — paralysis [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain spatial and temporal summation at synapses. (6)
questions.solution:
A single impulse may not release enough neurotransmitter to reach threshold [B1]
Spatial summation: several presynaptic neurones release neurotransmitter onto one postsynaptic neurone [B1]
Their combined effect can reach threshold [B1]
Temporal summation: one neurone fires several impulses in quick succession [B1]
Neurotransmitter builds up in the cleft, reaching threshold [B1]
Allows integration of signals / filters out weak stimuli [B1]

questions.prompt: TTX slows conduction in Purkyne fibres. Suggest and explain the effect on the heartbeat. (3)
questions.solution:
Impulses spread more slowly through the ventricles [B1]
Ventricles contract less synchronously / not from the apex upwards [B1]
Less forceful contraction / reduced stroke volume / irregular or slower heartbeat [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why transmission of action potentials is slower along unmyelinated axons. (3)
questions.solution:
No myelin sheath, so depolarisation must occur along the whole length of the axon [B1]
No saltatory conduction between nodes of Ranvier [B1]
More time needed for many successive depolarisations [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why multiple sclerosis, which damages myelin, causes muscle weakness and loss of coordination. (3)
questions.solution:
Myelin damaged, so saltatory conduction lost [B1]
Impulses slowed or blocked / may jump between neurones [B1]
Muscles don't receive impulses correctly, so weakness and poor coordination [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the structures in a synaptic knob that store neurotransmitter. (1)
questions.solution: Synaptic vesicles [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why synaptic knobs contain many mitochondria. (1)
questions.solution: To produce ATP for exocytosis of vesicles / resynthesis of neurotransmitter / active transport [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why impulses can only pass in one direction across a synapse. (1)
questions.solution: Vesicles of neurotransmitter are only in the presynaptic knob and receptors only on the postsynaptic membrane [B1]

questions.prompt:
(i) Name the gap between two neurones at a synapse. (1)
(ii) Give one feature visible in an electron micrograph that shows which neurone is presynaptic. (1)
(iii) Name the type of feedback involved in the rapid opening of sodium channels during depolarisation, and the term for the reversal of membrane polarity. (2)
questions.solution:
(i) Synaptic cleft [B1]
(ii) Presynaptic neurone contains synaptic vesicles / many mitochondria [B1]
(iii) Positive feedback [B1]
Depolarisation [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how a Pacinian corpuscle converts pressure into a generator potential. (4)
questions.solution:
Pressure deforms the layers of connective tissue (lamellae) [B1]
Stretch-mediated Na⁺ channels in the neurone membrane open [B1]
Na⁺ diffuses in, producing a generator potential [B1]
If threshold is reached, an action potential is triggered [B1]

questions.prompt: Compare the structures of sensory, relay and motor neurones. (4)
questions.solution:
Sensory: cell body to the side, long dendron and short axon [B1]
Relay: short, many dendrites, in the CNS [B1]
Motor: cell body in the CNS, long axon to effector [B1]
All have a cell body, axon and dendrites; sensory and motor often myelinated [B1]

questions.prompt:
Gestational diabetes causes high blood glucose even though insulin is produced normally.

(i) Name the type of diabetes most similar to this, and explain. (2)
(ii) Suggest two ways of managing it. (2)
hints: Insulin is made but cells don't respond.
questions.solution:
(i) Type 2 [B1]
Insulin is produced but target cells respond less (insulin resistance) [B1]
(ii) Controlled diet low in sugar / regular carbohydrate intake [B1]
Exercise / monitor blood glucose / drugs (e.g. metformin) / insulin injections if needed [B1]

questions.prompt: Compare type 1 and type 2 diabetes. (4)
questions.solution:
Type 1: β cells destroyed by autoimmune response, so no insulin made [B1]
Type 1 usually develops in childhood; treated with insulin injections [B1]
Type 2: cells become resistant to insulin / β cells make less [B1]
Type 2 linked to obesity / lifestyle; treated with diet, exercise, drugs [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how human insulin is produced using genetically modified bacteria, and give two advantages over insulin from pigs. (4)
questions.solution:
Human insulin gene inserted into bacterial plasmids, which are taken up by bacteria [B1]
Bacteria cultured in fermenters, insulin extracted and purified [B1]
Advantage: identical to human insulin, so fewer allergic reactions / works faster [B1]
Advantage: cheaper / large quantities / no ethical or religious objections [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why anabolic steroids can be effective when applied to the skin. (2)
questions.solution:
Steroids are lipid-soluble, so diffuse through the phospholipid bilayers of skin cells [B1]
Enter the blood and reach target cells [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how testosterone affects its target cells. (2)
questions.solution:
Testosterone diffuses into the cell and binds to a receptor in the cytoplasm [B1]
Hormone–receptor complex acts as a transcription factor, switching on genes [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how urine samples can be tested for anabolic steroids. (2)
questions.solution:
Gas chromatography separates substances in the sample [B1]
Mass spectrometry identifies them by their mass / compared with known standards [B1]

questions.prompt:
(i) Name the region of the adrenal gland that secretes adrenaline. (1)
(ii) Give two effects of adrenaline on the body. (2)
questions.solution:
(i) Medulla [B1]
(ii) Two of: increases heart rate; increases breathing rate; dilates pupils; raises blood glucose (glycogenolysis); diverts blood to muscles [B1 B1]

questions.prompt: Name three hormones secreted by the adrenal cortex and give a role for each. (3)
questions.solution:
Cortisol — regulates metabolism / stress response / raises blood glucose [B1]
Aldosterone — controls Na⁺ reabsorption and blood pressure [B1]
Androgens — sex hormones, e.g. growth of pubic hair [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the structure of the adrenal gland. (3)
questions.solution:
Outer capsule [B1]
Cortex — outer region, divided into layers, secretes steroid hormones [B1]
Medulla — inner region, secretes adrenaline and noradrenaline [B1]

questions.prompt:
(i) Describe what is meant by an endocrine gland. (2)
(ii) Explain why the cells of the pancreas that make digestive enzymes are exocrine. (1)
questions.solution:
(i) A ductless gland [B1]
That secretes hormones directly into the blood [B1]
(ii) They secrete enzymes into a duct (pancreatic duct), not the blood [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the histology of the pancreas. (3)
questions.solution:
Mostly exocrine acini — groups of cells secreting digestive enzymes into ducts [B1]
Islets of Langerhans scattered between them [B1]
Islets contain α cells (glucagon) and β cells (insulin) [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how β cells secrete insulin when blood glucose rises. (3)
questions.solution:
Glucose enters β cells and is respired, raising ATP [B1]
ATP closes K⁺ channels, depolarising the membrane [B1]
Voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels open; Ca²⁺ triggers exocytosis of insulin vesicles [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest where receptors for steroid hormones are found in target cells, and give a reason. (2)
questions.solution:
Inside the cell — in the cytoplasm or nucleus [B1]
Steroids are lipid-soluble, so can diffuse through the cell membrane [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest where receptors for insulin are found and give a reason. (2)
questions.solution:
On the cell surface membrane [B1]
Insulin is a large, water-soluble protein, so cannot cross the phospholipid bilayer [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why hormones can have widespread effects while only affecting target cells. (2)
questions.solution:
Hormones travel in the blood to all parts of the body [B1]
Only cells with complementary receptors respond [B1]

questions.prompt:
(i) Adrenal failure causes fatigue, weight loss, low blood pressure and salt craving. Explain these symptoms. (2)
(ii) Explain why patients with a pituitary tumour may have adrenal cortex failure but still respond normally to danger. (3)
hints: ACTH vs nervous control of the medulla.
questions.solution:
(i) Low aldosterone means less Na⁺ reabsorbed, so salt lost and blood volume / pressure falls [B1]
Low cortisol means less glucose mobilised — fatigue / weight loss [B1]
(ii) Pituitary makes ACTH, which stimulates the adrenal cortex [B1]
So the tumour reduces cortex hormones [B1]
But the adrenal medulla is stimulated by sympathetic nerves, so adrenaline is still released [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how the hypothalamus, pituitary and adrenal glands work together in the response to long-term stress. (5)
questions.solution:
Hypothalamus releases CRH [B1]
CRH stimulates the anterior pituitary to release ACTH [B1]
ACTH travels in the blood to the adrenal cortex [B1]
Adrenal cortex releases cortisol [B1]
Cortisol raises blood glucose / suppresses inflammation; negative feedback on the hypothalamus [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the fight or flight response. (5)
questions.solution:
Hypothalamus activates the sympathetic nervous system [B1]
Adrenal medulla releases adrenaline [B1]
Heart rate and breathing rate increase [B1]
Blood glucose rises (glycogenolysis); blood diverted to muscles [B1]
Pupils dilate; airways dilate [B1]

questions.prompt:
(i) Suggest how the startle reflex of a newborn baby helps prevent harm. (2)
(ii) Describe the blinking reflex when an object moves towards a child's eyes, and explain its advantage. (3)
questions.solution:
(i) Baby throws out arms and clings / cries, so the parent is alerted [B1]
Reduces risk of falling [B1]
(ii) Light / movement detected by the retina; impulses to the brain (cranial reflex) [B1]
Motor impulses cause eyelid muscles to close (blink) [B1]
Rapid, involuntary — protects the eye from damage [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the knee-jerk reflex and explain why it is useful. (5)
questions.solution:
Tapping below the kneecap stretches the quadriceps [B1]
Stretch receptors send impulses along a sensory neurone to the spinal cord [B1]
Synapses directly with a motor neurone (no relay) [B1]
Quadriceps contracts, leg kicks forward [B1]
Helps maintain posture and balance; used to test nervous function [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the functions of the cerebrum, cerebellum, medulla oblongata, hypothalamus and pituitary gland. (5)
questions.solution:
Cerebrum — conscious thought, memory, voluntary actions [B1]
Cerebellum — coordination of movement and balance [B1]
Medulla — automatic control of heart rate and breathing [B1]
Hypothalamus — temperature and water balance [B1]
Pituitary — secretes hormones controlling other glands [B1]

questions.prompt: Where is auxin made in a shoot, and how does unilateral light affect its distribution? (1)
questions.solution: Made in the shoot tip; moves to the shaded side, causing more cell elongation there [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how auxin causes cell elongation in shoots. (1)
questions.solution: Auxin causes H⁺ to be pumped into cell walls; low pH activates expansins that loosen the cell wall so cells take up water and elongate [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why auxin causes shoots and roots to respond differently to gravity. (1)
questions.solution: Auxin builds up on the lower side; it stimulates elongation in shoots (bend up) but inhibits elongation in roots (bend down) [B1]

questions.prompt: Give the role of abscisic acid in a plant under water stress. (1)
questions.solution: Causes stomata to close, reducing water loss by transpiration [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the plant hormone that causes fruit ripening. (1)
questions.solution: Ethene (ethylene) [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the plant hormone that maintains seed dormancy. (1)
questions.solution: Abscisic acid [B1]

questions.prompt: Give one example of evidence for geotropism (gravitropism) in plants. (1)
questions.solution: Roots grow downwards / shoots grow upwards in the dark [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the tropism shown when a pea tendril coils around a support. (1)
questions.solution: Thigmotropism [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the tropism shown when roots grow towards water. (1)
questions.solution: Hydrotropism [B1]

questions.prompt: Name two plant hormones involved in controlling leaf fall (abscission). (1)
questions.solution: Auxin and ethene (cytokinins also involved) [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why deciduous trees lose their leaves in winter. (1)
questions.solution: Low light means little photosynthesis; dropping leaves saves energy / reduces water loss and frost damage [B1]

questions.prompt: Give one commercial use of ethene. (1)
questions.solution: Speeding up / controlling fruit ripening (e.g. bananas) / promoting fruit drop [B1]

questions.prompt:
Cabbage plants treated with gibberellin grew much taller stems than untreated plants.

Explain why gibberellin is classed as a plant hormone. (3)
hints: Made in one place, acts in another.
questions.solution:
It is a chemical made in one part of the plant [B1]
Transported to target cells elsewhere [B1]
Has an effect on growth / development in small amounts, by binding to receptors [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how gibberellins cause stem elongation. (3)
questions.solution:
Gibberellins stimulate cell elongation in the internodes [B1]
And cell division [B1]
By loosening cell walls / breaking down DELLA proteins that inhibit growth [B1]

questions.prompt: Compare plant hormones with animal hormones. (3)
questions.solution:
Both are chemical signals that act on target cells with receptors [B1]
Plant hormones are made in many tissues, not specialised glands [B1]
Plant hormones move by diffusion / active transport / in xylem and phloem; animal hormones in the blood [B1]

questions.prompt: Give one role of gibberellin in plants other than stem elongation. (1)
questions.solution: Seed germination (mobilising starch stores) / flowering / fruit growth / breaking dormancy [B1]

questions.prompt: Give one commercial use of gibberellin. (1)
questions.solution: Making grapes larger / delaying ripening / malting barley in brewing / increasing sugar cane yield [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why dwarf varieties of plants are often short. (1)
questions.solution: They have a mutation so they cannot make (enough) active gibberellin [B1]

questions.prompt:
(i) Explain why higher concentrations of auxin result in fewer side shoots. (1)
(ii) Give two commercial uses of auxins. (2)
questions.solution:
(i) Auxin inhibits the growth of lateral buds (apical dominance) [B1]
(ii) Two of: rooting powder for cuttings; selective weedkillers; seedless fruit (parthenocarpy); preventing fruit drop [B1 B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how synthetic auxins act as selective weedkillers. (3)
questions.solution:
Absorbed more by broad-leaved weeds than narrow-leaved grasses / cereals [B1]
Cause rapid, uncontrolled growth [B1]
So the weeds die, while crops are unaffected [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how rooting powder helps cuttings grow into new plants. (3)
questions.solution:
Rooting powder contains auxin [B1]
Stimulates root growth at the cut end [B1]
So the cutting can absorb water and minerals and survive [B1]

questions.prompt:
(i) Name three proteins found in the thin filaments of a sarcomere. (3)
(ii) Explain why the A band and I band look different in an electron micrograph. (2)
questions.solution:
(i) Actin [B1]
Troponin [B1]
Tropomyosin [B1]
(ii) A band contains thick myosin filaments (and overlapping actin), so appears dark [B1]
I band contains only thin actin filaments, so appears light [B1]

questions.prompt: Using the sliding filament model, explain how a sarcomere shortens and which bands change length. (5)
questions.solution:
Myosin heads bind to actin, forming cross-bridges [B1]
Heads pivot (power stroke), pulling actin towards the centre (M line) [B1]
ATP binds, myosin detaches; ATP hydrolysis re-cocks the head [B1]
I band and H zone shorten; Z lines move closer [B1]
A band stays the same length [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the events from an impulse arriving at the neuromuscular junction to the formation of actin–myosin cross-bridges. (5)
questions.solution:
Acetylcholine released and binds to receptors on the sarcolemma [B1]
Sarcolemma depolarises; depolarisation spreads down T-tubules [B1]
Ca²⁺ released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum [B1]
Ca²⁺ binds troponin, which moves tropomyosin off the binding sites on actin [B1]
Myosin heads bind to actin, forming cross-bridges [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why a lack of ATP after death causes muscles to become rigid (rigor mortis). (2)
hints: What does ATP do to cross-bridges?
questions.solution:
ATP is needed to detach myosin heads from actin [B1]
Without ATP, cross-bridges remain attached, so muscles stay contracted / stiff [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why ATP is also needed for muscle relaxation. (2)
questions.solution:
ATP is used to actively transport Ca²⁺ back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum [B1]
So tropomyosin blocks binding sites again and the muscle relaxes [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain the role of ATP hydrolysis in the power stroke of a myosin head. (2)
questions.solution:
Hydrolysis of ATP releases energy that returns (re-cocks) the myosin head to its upright position [B1]
So it can bind further along the actin and pull again [B1]

questions.prompt:
Mustard seeds were placed on damp paper in Petri dishes containing different IAA concentrations, standing vertically in the dark.

(i) Explain why the dishes were vertical and in the dark. (2)
(ii) Explain the purpose of a dish with distilled water only. (2)
questions.solution:
(i) Vertical so roots and shoots grow in straight lines for measuring / gravity acts equally [B1]
Dark so phototropism doesn't affect growth / only IAA affects growth [B1]
(ii) A control to show growth without IAA [B1]
So the effect of IAA can be compared / calculated [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why low concentrations of auxin stimulate root growth, while high concentrations inhibit it. (4)
questions.solution:
Roots are much more sensitive to auxin than shoots [B1]
Very low concentrations stimulate cell elongation in roots [B1]
Higher concentrations inhibit root elongation [B1]
The same high concentrations promote shoot elongation [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how auxin causes a horizontal root to grow downwards. (4)
hints: Auxin accumulates on the lower side.
questions.solution:
Gravity causes auxin to accumulate on the lower side of the root [B1]
High auxin inhibits cell elongation in roots [B1]
So upper side elongates more than the lower side [B1]
Root bends downwards (positive gravitropism) [B1]

questions.prompt:
(i) Outline the importance of photosynthetic pigments. (4)
(ii) Seaweeds that grow in deep water have pigments that absorb blue-green light. Suggest why. (1)
questions.solution:
(i) Pigments absorb light energy [B1]
Arranged in photosystems in the thylakoid membranes [B1]
Accessory pigments pass energy to chlorophyll a at the reaction centre [B1]
Electrons are excited and passed to the electron transport chain; a range of pigments absorbs a wider range of wavelengths [B1]
(ii) Red light is absorbed by water near the surface; only blue-green light penetrates deep water [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between an absorption spectrum and an action spectrum, and what their similarity shows. (5)
questions.solution:
Absorption spectrum shows the wavelengths of light absorbed by a pigment [B1]
Action spectrum shows the rate of photosynthesis at each wavelength [B1]
Both peak in blue and red light [B1]
The close match shows that absorbed light is used in photosynthesis [B1]
Green light is mostly reflected, so little photosynthesis at green wavelengths [B1]

questions.prompt:
A chromatogram of leaf pigments shows a spot that travelled 3.2 cm when the solvent travelled 8.0 cm.

(i) Calculate the Rf value. (2)
(ii) Explain how Rf values are used to identify pigments. (3)
questions.solution:
(i) 3.2 ÷ 8.0 [M1]
= 0.40 [A1]
(ii) Each pigment has a characteristic Rf value in a given solvent [B1]
Calculated values are compared with known values [B1]
Depends on solubility in the solvent and attraction to the stationary phase [B1]

questions.prompt: Seedlings took up oxygen at light intensities below 1500 lux but released oxygen above it. Explain why. (2)
questions.solution:
Below 1500 lux, respiration rate is greater than photosynthesis, so net O₂ uptake [B1]
Above it, photosynthesis exceeds respiration, so net O₂ release — about 1500 lux is the compensation point [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why shade plants have a lower compensation point than sun plants. (2)
questions.solution:
Shade plants have lower respiration rates [B1]
And more efficient light capture (more chlorophyll / larger leaves), so photosynthesis matches respiration at lower light [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why plants cannot grow if kept at their compensation point. (2)
questions.solution:
All glucose made is used in respiration [B1]
No net gain in carbohydrate / biomass for growth [B1]

questions.prompt: Cyanobacteria appear blue-green. Explain why. (1)
questions.solution: Their pigments absorb red (and other) wavelengths and reflect / transmit blue-green light [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why plants have several different photosynthetic pigments. (1)
questions.solution: Each pigment absorbs different wavelengths, so together they absorb a wider range of light for photosynthesis [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the primary photosynthetic pigment found in the reaction centre of a photosystem. (1)
questions.solution: Chlorophyll a [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the light-independent stage (Calvin cycle) of photosynthesis, naming the molecules involved. (4)
questions.solution:
CO₂ combines with RuBP (5C), catalysed by RuBisCO [B1]
Forms two molecules of GP (3C) [B1]
GP is reduced to triose phosphate (TP) using ATP and reduced NADP [B1]
Some TP used to make glucose, amino acids, lipids; most regenerates RuBP using ATP [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how triose phosphate is used to make other organic molecules in a plant. (4)
questions.solution:
Two TP combine to form hexose sugars (glucose), used to make sucrose, starch and cellulose [B1]
TP converted to glycerol, and acetyl CoA from GP / TP to fatty acids — lipids [B1]
GP / TP used to make amino acids, with nitrate as a nitrogen source [B1]
Proteins and enzymes made from amino acids [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why five out of every six molecules of triose phosphate made are used to regenerate RuBP. (4)
questions.solution:
RuBP is needed to accept more CO₂ [B1]
Six TP (18 C) are made for every three CO₂ fixed [B1]
Five TP (15 C) regenerate three RuBP (15 C) [B1]
Only one TP is a net gain for making other molecules [B1]

questions.prompt:
Oxygen concentration rose fastest at 25 °C and slowest at 10 °C. At 30 °C, it rose quickly at first then levelled off.

Describe and explain what these results show. (3)
questions.solution:
Rate increases with temperature up to about 25 °C [B1]
Enzymes of the Calvin cycle (RuBisCO) have more kinetic energy, so more enzyme–substrate complexes [B1]
At 30 °C, enzymes begin to denature / photorespiration increases / CO₂ becomes limiting [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain the term limiting factor, using light intensity as an example. (3)
questions.solution:
The factor in shortest supply that limits the rate of a process [B1]
At low light, increasing light intensity increases the rate [B1]
At high light, rate levels off because another factor (CO₂ / temperature) is now limiting [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why measuring oxygen production underestimates the rate of photosynthesis. (3)
questions.solution:
The plant respires, using some oxygen [B1]
Some oxygen dissolves in the water [B1]
So the measured rate is net, not gross photosynthesis [B1]

questions.prompt:
(i) Explain why calling the light-independent stage the "dark reaction" is partly accurate and partly inaccurate. (2)
(ii) Name the enzyme that fixes CO₂. (1)
hints: Does it happen in the dark?
questions.solution:
(i) Accurate: light is not used directly [B1]
Inaccurate: it needs ATP and reduced NADP from the light-dependent stage, so stops soon after dark [B1]
(ii) RuBisCO [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe cyclic photophosphorylation and explain how it differs from non-cyclic photophosphorylation. (3)
questions.solution:
Only photosystem I is involved; excited electrons return to PSI via the electron transport chain [B1]
ATP is made, but no reduced NADP and no oxygen [B1]
Non-cyclic involves PSI and PSII, photolysis of water, producing ATP, reduced NADP and O₂ [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how ATP is made by chemiosmosis in chloroplasts. (3)
questions.solution:
Energy from electrons passing along the ETC pumps H⁺ into the thylakoid space [B1]
H⁺ also come from photolysis, creating a concentration gradient [B1]
H⁺ diffuse back through ATP synthase into the stroma, producing ATP [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the location and function of each of these parts of a chloroplast: envelope, stroma, intergranal lamellae, starch grains. (4)
questions.solution:
Envelope — double outer membrane controlling what enters and leaves [B1]
Stroma — fluid site of the light-independent reactions [B1]
Intergranal lamellae — thylakoid membranes linking grana [B1]
Starch grains — store carbohydrate made in photosynthesis [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the structure of a photosystem. (4)
questions.solution:
Found in the thylakoid membranes [B1]
Light-harvesting (antenna) complex of many pigment molecules [B1]
Absorb light and pass energy to the reaction centre [B1]
Reaction centre contains chlorophyll a, which releases excited electrons [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe photolysis and explain its importance. (4)
questions.solution:
Light splits water into H⁺, electrons and oxygen [B1]
Occurs at photosystem II [B1]
Electrons replace those lost from PSII chlorophyll [B1]
H⁺ used to reduce NADP; O₂ released as a by-product [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the Calvin cycle, naming each molecule. (5)
questions.solution:
CO₂ combines with RuBP (5C) catalysed by RuBisCO [B1]
Unstable 6C intermediate splits into two GP (3C) [B1]
GP reduced to TP using reduced NADP and ATP [B1]
Two TP combine to form hexose phosphate, transported as sucrose [B1]
Most TP used to regenerate RuBP using ATP [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how the light-dependent and light-independent stages of photosynthesis are linked. (5)
hints: Products of one used in the other.
questions.solution:
Light-dependent stage produces ATP and reduced NADP [B1]
These are used in the Calvin cycle to reduce GP to TP [B1]
ATP also used to regenerate RuBP [B1]
ADP, Pi and NADP return to the thylakoids [B1]
So the light-independent stage stops soon after light is removed [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how Calvin used radioactive carbon dioxide to work out the order of reactions in the light-independent stage. (5)
questions.solution:
Algae (Chlorella) supplied with ¹⁴CO₂ in the light [B1]
Samples taken at short time intervals and killed in hot methanol [B1]
Compounds separated by chromatography [B1]
Radioactive compounds detected by autoradiography [B1]
The first to become radioactive was GP, then TP, then hexoses — showing the sequence [B1]

questions.prompt:
(i) Name a tissue, other than skeletal muscle, that takes up glucose in response to insulin. (1)
(ii) Explain why glucose is needed for muscle contraction. (3)
questions.solution:
(i) Liver / adipose tissue [B1]
(ii) Glucose is used in respiration to make ATP [B1]
ATP needed for myosin heads to detach from actin and re-cock [B1]
ATP needed to pump Ca²⁺ back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how glycogen in muscle cells is used during exercise. (4)
questions.solution:
Glycogen is hydrolysed to glucose (glycogenolysis) [B1]
Stimulated by adrenaline [B1]
Glucose used in glycolysis and respiration [B1]
Producing ATP for contraction [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain the role of creatine phosphate in muscles. (4)
questions.solution:
Creatine phosphate donates a phosphate group to ADP [B1]
Regenerating ATP very quickly [B1]
Without needing oxygen [B1]
Supplies ATP for short bursts of intense exercise (a few seconds); replenished during rest [B1]

questions.prompt: Three genera of ants had RQs of 1.0, 0.7 and 0.9. Suggest the main respiratory substrate of each and justify. (3)
questions.solution:
RQ 1.0 — carbohydrate (e.g. nectar / honeydew) [B1]
RQ 0.7 — lipid / fat [B1]
RQ 0.9 — protein (e.g. insects) [B1]

questions.prompt: An organism produced 24 cm³ of CO₂ and used 30 cm³ of O₂ in 10 minutes. Calculate the RQ and suggest the respiratory substrate. (3)
questions.solution:
24 ÷ 30 [M1]
= 0.8 [A1]
A mixture of lipid and protein / protein [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why lipids release more energy per gram than carbohydrates or proteins. (3)
questions.solution:
Lipids contain more hydrogen atoms per gram [B1]
More reduced NAD / FAD formed [B1]
So more ATP made in oxidative phosphorylation [B1]

questions.prompt: Outline how ATP is generated by chemiosmosis in mitochondria, using glucose as the respiratory substrate. (6)
questions.solution:
Glycolysis, link reaction and Krebs cycle produce reduced NAD and FAD [B1]
These release hydrogen atoms at the inner mitochondrial membrane, split into H⁺ and electrons [B1]
Electrons pass along the electron transport chain, releasing energy [B1]
Energy used to pump H⁺ into the intermembrane space, creating a gradient [B1]
H⁺ diffuse back through ATP synthase, producing ATP from ADP and Pi [B1]
Oxygen accepts electrons and H⁺, forming water [B1]
Level-marked (5–6 marks).

questions.prompt: Some chemicals make the inner mitochondrial membrane permeable to H⁺. Explain the effect on ATP production and body temperature. (6)
questions.solution:
H⁺ leak back across the membrane without passing through ATP synthase [B1]
Proton gradient is reduced [B1]
Less ATP is produced [B1]
Electron transport continues, so oxygen is still used [B1]
Energy is released as heat, so body temperature rises [B1]
Cells respire more substrate to compensate — weight loss / fatigue [B1]
Level-marked (5–6 marks).

questions.prompt: Explain why the theoretical yield of 38 ATP per glucose is rarely achieved. (6)
questions.solution:
Some H⁺ leak across the inner membrane [B1]
ATP used to transport pyruvate / ADP into the mitochondrion [B1]
Reduced NAD from glycolysis must be shuttled in, losing energy [B1]
Reduced FAD yields fewer ATP than reduced NAD [B1]
Actual yield is about 30–32 ATP [B1]
Some energy lost as heat [B1]
Level-marked (5–6 marks).

questions.prompt:
In a respirometer, liquid moved 15 mm in 30 minutes along a capillary of diameter 0.1 mm.

(i) Calculate the rate of oxygen uptake in mm³ h⁻¹, to 2 significant figures (V = πr²l). (3)
(ii) Gas production rose from 0.8 to 2.0 mm³ h⁻¹ as light increased. Calculate the percentage increase. (2)
(iii) Suggest why soda lime was not used for seedlings in the light. (1)
questions.solution:
(i) V = 3.14 × 0.05² × 15 = 0.118 mm³ [M1]
Per hour: × 2 [M1]
= 0.24 mm³ h⁻¹ [A1]
(ii) (2.0 − 0.8) ÷ 0.8 × 100 [M1]
= 150 % [A1]
(iii) Soda lime would absorb CO₂ needed for photosynthesis [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how a respirometer can be used to measure the rate of anaerobic respiration in yeast. (6)
questions.solution:
Use yeast in glucose solution with no oxygen (layer of oil / nitrogen gas) [B1]
Don't use soda lime, so CO₂ produced increases the volume [B1]
Liquid moves away from the yeast [B1]
Measure distance in a set time [B1]
Volume = πr²l [B1]
Control tube with boiled yeast; keep temperature constant [B1]

questions.prompt: Give three sources of error when using a simple respirometer and how to reduce each. (6)
questions.solution:
Temperature changes affect gas volume [B1]
Use a water bath / thermostatic control [B1]
Leaks in the apparatus [B1]
Seal joints with petroleum jelly / test with a known volume [B1]
Atmospheric pressure changes [B1]
Use a control tube / differential respirometer [B1]

questions.prompt: Brown fat cells have a high rate of aerobic respiration. Suggest which organelle is more numerous in these cells. (1)
questions.solution: Mitochondria [B1]

questions.prompt: Brown fat produces heat rather than ATP. Suggest how. (1)
questions.solution: A protein (thermogenin / UCP) lets H⁺ back through the inner membrane without passing through ATP synthase, so energy is released as heat [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why heart muscle cells have many mitochondria with densely packed cristae. (1)
questions.solution: Need lots of ATP for continuous contraction; more cristae give a larger surface area for oxidative phosphorylation [B1]

questions.prompt: Linoleic acid is oxidised: C₁₈H₃₂O₂ + 25 O₂ → 18 CO₂ + 16 H₂O. Calculate the respiratory quotient. (1)
Give the RQ for glucose and explain what an RQ above 1 shows. (1)
questions.solution: Glucose RQ = 1.0; above 1 shows some anaerobic respiration (CO₂ made without O₂ used) [B1]

questions.prompt: Give the typical RQ for proteins. (1)
questions.solution: About 0.9 [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest one reason why muscle fatigue occurs during intense exercise. (1)
questions.solution: Lactic acid build-up lowers pH / creatine phosphate depleted / ATP runs out [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why red blood cells can only respire anaerobically. (1)
questions.solution: They have no mitochondria, so only glycolysis (anaerobic) can occur [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why there is no net gas exchange by a leaf at the compensation point. (1)
questions.solution: Rate of photosynthesis equals rate of respiration, so O₂ and CO₂ produced are used at equal rates [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the different sources of ATP used in muscle contraction during strenuous exercise. (6)
questions.solution:
ATP already in muscle lasts only a few seconds [B1]
Creatine phosphate donates phosphate to ADP to regenerate ATP quickly (about 10 s) [B1]
Anaerobic respiration — glycolysis; pyruvate reduced to lactate to regenerate NAD [B1]
Produces 2 ATP per glucose quickly, but lactate causes fatigue [B1]
Aerobic respiration produces most ATP (about 30 per glucose) via oxidative phosphorylation [B1]
Needs oxygen; slower to supply ATP; uses glycogen and fats [B1]
Level-marked (5–6 marks).

questions.prompt: Describe glycolysis and the link reaction. (6)
questions.solution:
Glucose phosphorylated by 2 ATP to hexose bisphosphate [B1]
Split into two triose phosphate (TP) molecules [B1]
TP oxidised to pyruvate; NAD reduced; 4 ATP made (net 2) [B1]
Pyruvate enters the mitochondrial matrix by active transport [B1]
Link reaction: pyruvate decarboxylated and dehydrogenated (reduced NAD formed) [B1]
Acetyl group combines with coenzyme A to form acetyl CoA [B1]
Level-marked (5–6 marks).

questions.prompt: Describe oxidative phosphorylation. (6)
questions.solution:
Reduced NAD and FAD release H atoms, which split into H⁺ and electrons [B1]
Electrons pass along carriers in the inner mitochondrial membrane [B1]
Energy released pumps H⁺ into the intermembrane space [B1]
H⁺ diffuse back through ATP synthase (chemiosmosis), making ATP [B1]
Oxygen is the final electron acceptor, forming water [B1]
Produces most ATP in aerobic respiration [B1]
Level-marked (5–6 marks).

questions.prompt:
Oxygen consumption of a fish was measured using a chamber with water flowing through, with oxygen probes at the inlet and outlet linked to a computer.

(i) Suggest two modifications to investigate the effect of temperature on respiration. (2)
(ii) Give one advantage of using a computer to collect data. (1)
(iii) Explain one reason, other than continuous monitoring, why a constant water flow is needed. (2)
(iv) Suggest and explain one other precaution to ensure valid results. (2)
questions.solution:
(i) Place chamber in a thermostatically controlled water bath [B1]
Use water at several different temperatures; allow time to acclimatise [B1]
(ii) Readings at regular, frequent intervals with no human error / data stored automatically [B1]
(iii) Keeps oxygen supplied / removes CO₂ and waste [B1]
So oxygen doesn't become limiting / fish isn't stressed [B1]
(iv) Fish should be inactive / not fed beforehand / same fish mass [B1]
Because activity and digestion increase respiration rate [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how a simple respirometer can be used to measure the rate of oxygen uptake by germinating peas. (7)
questions.solution:
Place peas in a tube with soda lime (to absorb CO₂) [B1]
Connect to a capillary tube containing coloured liquid [B1]
Set up a control tube with glass beads of the same volume [B1]
Place in a water bath at constant temperature; allow to equilibrate [B1]
Oxygen uptake reduces the volume, so liquid moves towards the peas [B1]
Measure distance moved in a set time; volume = πr² × distance [B1]
Repeat and calculate rate per gram of peas [B1]

questions.prompt:
(i) In a respirometer, liquid moved 24 mm in 10 minutes along a capillary tube of radius 0.5 mm. Calculate the rate of oxygen uptake in mm³ min⁻¹. (3)
(ii) Explain why a control tube is used. (2)
(iii) Explain how a respirometer can be used to measure the RQ. (2)
questions.solution:
(i) Volume = 3.14 × 0.25 × 24 [M1]
= 18.8 mm³ [M1]
Rate = 1.88 mm³ min⁻¹ [A1]
(ii) To account for changes in temperature / pressure [B1]
So the movement measured is due only to respiration [B1]
(iii) Measure O₂ uptake with soda lime; then without soda lime to find CO₂ – O₂ difference [B1]
Calculate CO₂ produced ÷ O₂ used [B1]

questions.prompt:
The largest fish consumed 90 mg O₂ h⁻¹ at 13 °C and 205 mg O₂ h⁻¹ at 23 °C. Growth was best at 18 °C.

(i) Calculate Q₁₀ to 3 significant figures. (2)
(ii) Evaluate the conclusion that 18 °C is the best temperature for farming these fish. (4)
hints: Q₁₀ = rate at T + 10 ÷ rate at T.
questions.solution:
(i) 205 ÷ 90 [M1]
= 2.28 [A1]
(ii) Respiration rate is high at 23 °C, so more food energy used for respiration rather than growth [B1]
At 13 °C metabolism and growth are slow; 18 °C may balance these [B1]
But only three temperatures tested; optimum may lie between them [B1]
Cost of heating water / effect on oxygen solubility / only fish of certain sizes tested [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why the respiration rate of ectothermic fish increases with water temperature, and why it falls at very high temperatures. (6)
questions.solution:
Fish are ectotherms, so body temperature follows water temperature [B1]
Respiratory enzymes have more kinetic energy [B1]
More enzyme–substrate complexes form [B1]
Rate roughly doubles per 10 °C (Q₁₀ ≈ 2) [B1]
At very high temperatures enzymes denature [B1]
Less oxygen dissolves in warm water [B1]
Level-marked (5–6 marks).

questions.prompt:
The rate of respiration of yeast was 12 units at 15 °C, 26 units at 25 °C and 50 units at 35 °C.

Calculate Q₁₀ between 15 and 25 °C, and between 25 and 35 °C, and explain the results. (6)
questions.solution:
26 ÷ 12 = 2.17 [M1 A1]
50 ÷ 26 = 1.92 [M1 A1]
Both about 2 — rate roughly doubles per 10 °C, typical of enzyme-controlled reactions [B1]
Slightly lower Q₁₀ at higher temperature as enzymes approach their optimum [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the role of Hox genes. (1)
questions.solution: Code for transcription factors that control the development of the body plan (which body parts form where) [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why Hox genes are similar in very different animals such as fruit flies and humans. (1)
questions.solution: They are highly conserved — mutations would disrupt development and be lethal, so they are selected against [B1]

questions.prompt: A homeobox is 180 base pairs long. How many amino acids does it code for? (1)
questions.solution: 60 amino acids [B1]

questions.prompt: Two homeoboxes of 180 bp differ in 3 base pairs. What is the minimum number of amino acids that could differ? (1)
Two homeoboxes of 180 bp differ in 3 base pairs (all substitutions). What is the maximum number of amino acids that could differ? (1)
Explain why a substitution mutation may have no effect on a protein. (1)
questions.solution: The genetic code is degenerate, so the new codon may code for the same amino acid [B1]

questions.prompt:
In sickle cell anaemia, a codon in the β-globin mRNA changes from GAG to GUG.

(i) Using the genetic code (GAG = glutamic acid, GUG = valine), describe the effect on the protein. (1)
(ii) Outline the role of RNA polymerase in making mRNA. (2)
(iii) Give the anticodon of the tRNA that brings valine to the codon GUG. (1)
(iv) What type of mutation causes this change? (1)
questions.solution:
(i) Glutamic acid replaced by valine [B1]
(ii) RNA polymerase binds to the promoter and moves along the template strand [B1]
Joins free RNA nucleotides complementary to the template, forming phosphodiester bonds [B1]
(iii) CAC [B1]
(iv) Substitution (point) mutation [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the process of translation. (5)
questions.solution:
mRNA binds to a ribosome [B1]
tRNA with a complementary anticodon pairs with the start codon (AUG), carrying methionine [B1]
A second tRNA brings the next amino acid; a peptide bond forms between amino acids (using ATP) [B1]
Ribosome moves along the mRNA one codon at a time [B1]
Continues until a stop codon; polypeptide released [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the process of transcription. (5)
questions.solution:
DNA helicase / RNA polymerase unwinds the gene, breaking hydrogen bonds [B1]
One strand acts as the template [B1]
Free RNA nucleotides pair with complementary bases (U with A) [B1]
RNA polymerase joins them, forming pre-mRNA [B1]
Introns removed by splicing; mRNA leaves the nucleus via a nuclear pore [B1]

questions.prompt: Using your knowledge of the genetic code and protein structure, explain why some gene mutations do not affect the function of a protein. (6)
questions.solution:
The code is degenerate — a substitution may produce a codon for the same amino acid (silent mutation) [B1]
A new amino acid with a similar R group may not change folding (conservative) [B1]
The change may be outside the active site / binding site [B1]
So the tertiary structure and function are unaffected [B1]
Mutation may be in an intron / non-coding region [B1]
Frameshifts near the end of a gene affect few amino acids; some mutations are beneficial or neutral [B1]
Level-marked (5–6 marks).

questions.prompt: Describe the different types of gene mutation and their possible effects on proteins. (6)
questions.solution:
Substitution: one base replaced by another [B1]
May be silent (same amino acid), missense (different amino acid) or nonsense (stop codon) [B1]
Insertion or deletion of a base causes a frameshift [B1]
All following codons change, usually giving a non-functional protein [B1]
Insertions / deletions of three bases add / remove one amino acid [B1]
Effects range from beneficial to harmful to neutral [B1]
Level-marked (5–6 marks).

questions.prompt: Describe how genes can be regulated at the transcriptional, post-transcriptional and post-translational levels. (6)
questions.solution:
Transcriptional: transcription factors bind promoters to switch genes on or off [B1]
e.g. lac operon in E. coli — repressor and lactose [B1]
Post-transcriptional: splicing of pre-mRNA to remove introns [B1]
Alternative splicing produces different proteins [B1]
Post-translational: proteins activated by modification, e.g. phosphorylation by kinases [B1]
cAMP activates protein kinase A [B1]
Level-marked (5–6 marks).

questions.prompt:
(i) Name the type of gene that controls the body plan of multicellular organisms. (1)
(ii) Describe apoptosis and explain its role in development. (5)
questions.solution:
(i) Homeobox (Hox) genes [B1]
(ii) Apoptosis is programmed cell death [B1]
Enzymes break down the cytoskeleton; the cell shrinks and DNA is broken down [B1]
Cell breaks into vesicles that are engulfed by phagocytes [B1]
Removes unwanted cells, e.g. tissue between fingers, excess neurones [B1]
Controlled by genes / signals; balances mitosis [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how Hox genes control body plan development. (6)
questions.solution:
Hox genes contain a homeobox — a 180 bp sequence [B1]
Code for a homeodomain protein (60 amino acids) [B1]
Which acts as a transcription factor, binding DNA [B1]
Switching on / off genes that control development of body segments [B1]
Hox genes are arranged in the order of the body parts they control [B1]
Highly conserved across animals [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how stress and the environment can affect body plan development and gene expression. (6)
questions.solution:
Internal stimuli (e.g. hormones) and external stimuli (temperature, drugs) affect gene expression [B1]
Stress can trigger apoptosis or change the rate of mitosis [B1]
e.g. drugs such as thalidomide disrupted limb development [B1]
Temperature can affect sex determination in some reptiles [B1]
Changes in transcription factors alter which genes are expressed [B1]
Balance between mitosis and apoptosis determines tissue shape [B1]
Level-marked (5–6 marks).

questions.prompt: Name three processes associated with sexual reproduction that produce genetic variation. (1)
questions.solution: Crossing over, independent assortment, random fertilisation [B1]

questions.prompt: Is gene mutation a source of variation only in sexual reproduction? Explain. (1)
questions.solution: No — mutations occur in all organisms during DNA replication, so are a source of variation in asexual reproduction too [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why random fertilisation increases genetic variation. (1)
questions.solution: Any male gamete can fuse with any female gamete, creating new combinations of alleles [B1]

questions.prompt: Wingspan of albatrosses varies from 2.5 m to 3.5 m. Is this intraspecific or interspecific variation, and is it caused by genes, the environment or both? (1)
questions.solution: Intraspecific; caused by both genes and environment [B1]

questions.prompt: Give one example of variation caused only by the environment. (1)
questions.solution: e.g. scars / tattoos / language spoken [B1]

questions.prompt: Give one example of discontinuous variation in humans. (1)
questions.solution: Blood group / tongue rolling / sex [B1]

questions.prompt: In a school, 12 % of students cannot roll their tongues (recessive). Use the Hardy-Weinberg equation to calculate the percentage who are heterozygous. (1)
If 36 % of a population show a recessive phenotype, what is the frequency of the dominant allele? (1)
State what p² represents in the Hardy-Weinberg equation. (1)
questions.solution: The frequency of the homozygous dominant genotype [B1]

questions.prompt: The gametes of a frog contain 10 chromosomes. Calculate the number of genetically different gametes that can be produced by independent assortment alone. (2)
Humans have 23 pairs of chromosomes. Calculate the number of possible combinations of chromosomes in gametes from independent assortment, in standard form. (2)
Explain why the number of genetically different gametes is actually far greater than 2ⁿ. (2)
questions.solution:
Crossing over between homologous chromosomes creates new combinations of alleles [B1]
Mutations also add new alleles [B1]

questions.prompt: Give one valid concern about growing genetically modified herbicide-resistant crops. (1)
questions.solution: Herbicide-resistance genes may spread to wild relatives, producing superweeds / reduced biodiversity [B1]

questions.prompt: Give one benefit of genetically modified pest-resistant crops. (1)
questions.solution: Higher yields / less insecticide sprayed [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why some people are concerned about large companies patenting GM seeds. (1)
questions.solution: Farmers in poorer countries may not afford the seeds / can't save seeds to replant [B1]

questions.prompt:
Students extracted DNA from leek leaves.
(i) Why were the leaves ground? (1)
(ii) Why was protease added? (1)
(iii) Why was detergent used? (1)
(iv) Why was ice-cold ethanol added? (1)
(v) Name the process by which DNA comes out of solution. (1)
hints: Break cells, remove histones, dissolve membranes.
questions.solution:
(i) To break cell walls / release cell contents [B1]
(ii) To break down histone proteins associated with DNA / enzymes that would damage DNA [B1]
(iii) To break down cell / nuclear membranes (lipids) [B1]
(iv) DNA is insoluble in cold ethanol, so it comes out of solution [B1]
(v) Precipitation [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why each of these is added in DNA extraction: salt, a water bath at 60 °C, then ice. Also explain why pineapple juice is a poor source of protease. (5)
questions.solution:
Salt causes DNA to clump / neutralises its charge [B1]
60 °C denatures DNase enzymes that would break down DNA [B1]
Ice stops further denaturation / slows enzyme activity [B1]
Pineapple juice also contains other substances / enzymes / variable protease activity [B1]
So the DNA would be impure [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how DNA is sequenced using the chain-termination method. (5)
questions.solution:
DNA mixed with primer, DNA polymerase, normal nucleotides and fluorescently labelled terminator nucleotides [B1]
DNA polymerase copies the template until a terminator is added, stopping synthesis [B1]
Produces fragments of every length, each ending in a labelled base [B1]
Fragments separated by size using capillary electrophoresis [B1]
Laser detects the colour of each fragment's end, giving the sequence [B1]

questions.prompt: Give three differences between somatic and germ line gene therapy. (3)
questions.solution:
Somatic targets body cells; germ line targets gametes / embryos [B1]
Somatic changes aren't inherited; germ line changes are passed to offspring [B1]
Somatic effects are temporary and need repeating; germ line is permanent [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how gene therapy could be used to treat cystic fibrosis. (3)
questions.solution:
Normal CFTR allele inserted into a vector (liposome / modified virus) [B1]
Delivered to airway epithelial cells, e.g. by inhaler / nasal spray [B1]
Cells express the normal allele, making functional CFTR protein [B1]

questions.prompt: Give three problems with gene therapy. (3)
questions.solution:
Difficult to get the gene into enough target cells [B1]
Viral vectors may cause immune responses / infections [B1]
Effects are short-lived and need repeating [B1]
Inserted gene may disrupt other genes, e.g. causing cancer [B1]
Any 3 — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt:
(i) Explain how inserting a new gene into a chromosome could affect other genes. (2)
(ii) Explain why gene therapy is unlikely to treat Huntington's disease, caused by a dominant allele. (1)
questions.solution:
(i) The gene may be inserted into another gene, disrupting its base sequence [B1]
Could switch on an oncogene / switch off a tumour suppressor gene, causing cancer [B1]
(ii) Adding a normal allele won't help — the dominant faulty allele is still expressed [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how CRISPR-Cas9 could be used to correct a faulty allele. (3)
questions.solution:
Guide RNA complementary to the target sequence directs Cas9 to the faulty allele [B1]
Cas9 cuts both DNA strands at that point [B1]
A template of the correct sequence is used by the cell to repair the cut [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how genetic screening could be used by a family affected by Huntington's disease. (3)
questions.solution:
Adults can be tested to see if they have the allele before symptoms [B1]
Embryos can be tested by PGD during IVF and unaffected embryos implanted [B1]
Prenatal testing (CVS / amniocentesis) — informed decisions; ethical issues as no cure exists [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how DNA fragments from a restriction digest are loaded and separated in gel electrophoresis. (1)
questions.solution: Samples loaded into wells at the cathode (negative) end; a current is passed and fragments move towards the anode [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why restriction enzymes cut DNA only at particular sites. (1)
questions.solution: Their active site is complementary to a specific base sequence (recognition site) [B1]

questions.prompt: Why are DNA bands stained or labelled after electrophoresis? (1)
questions.solution: DNA is invisible, so it is stained / labelled with a fluorescent or radioactive probe to show the bands [B1]

questions.prompt: Give one disadvantage of asexual reproduction for a population of coral. (1)
questions.solution: Offspring are genetically identical, so all are equally vulnerable to disease / environmental change [B1]

questions.prompt: Give one advantage of asexual reproduction. (1)
questions.solution: Fast / no mate needed / successful genotypes preserved in a stable environment [B1]

questions.prompt: Which type of cell division produces offspring by asexual reproduction? (1)
questions.solution: Mitosis [B1]

questions.prompt:
In frog cloning, the nucleus of an egg cell is destroyed and replaced with the nucleus of a tadpole intestine cell.

(i) Describe how the egg nucleus can be removed. (2)
(ii) Give one difference between this and the method used to clone Dolly the sheep. (1)
(iii) Suggest why the cloned frog is not a complete clone of the donor tadpole. (1)
questions.solution:
(i) Egg nucleus destroyed by UV light / removed with a micropipette (enucleation) [B1]
Under a microscope [B1]
(ii) Dolly: whole adult body cell fused with the enucleated egg using an electric current; embryo implanted in a surrogate [B1]
(iii) Mitochondrial DNA comes from the egg, not the tadpole [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe artificial embryo twinning in cattle. (4)
questions.solution:
Egg fertilised (IVF or naturally) and embryo allowed to divide [B1]
Early embryo split into several parts before cells specialise [B1]
Each part grows into an embryo [B1]
Embryos implanted into surrogate mothers, producing identical offspring [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how somatic cell nuclear transfer is carried out. (4)
questions.solution:
Nucleus removed from an egg cell [B1]
Body (somatic) cell from the animal to be cloned is fused with the empty egg using an electric current [B1]
Stimulated to divide; embryo develops [B1]
Implanted into a surrogate mother [B1]

questions.prompt:
A student concluded that Dolly's health problems were caused by using an adult donor nucleus. Evidence: cloning success was lower using nuclei from older donors in mouse and frog studies.

(i) Suggest why the graph shows the developmental stage of the donor rather than its age. (2)
(ii) Give three reasons why these data do not support the student's conclusion. (3)
questions.solution:
(i) Species have very different lifespans [B1]
So the developmental stage is comparable, while age is not [B1]
(ii) Data are from mice and frogs, not sheep [B1]
Data show success rates, not health of clones [B1]
No statistical analysis / small samples / correlation only [B1]

questions.prompt: Discuss the arguments for and against animal cloning. (5)
questions.solution:
For: produces many animals with desirable traits quickly [B1]
For: conserving endangered species / producing GM animals for medicines [B1]
Against: low success rate; many embryos die [B1]
Against: clones may have health problems / shorter lives [B1]
Against: reduces genetic diversity — vulnerable to disease [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why cloned animals made from adult cells might age faster. (5)
questions.solution:
Telomeres shorten each time a cell divides [B1]
Adult donor cells have already divided many times [B1]
So clones start life with shorter telomeres [B1]
Cells reach their division limit sooner [B1]
Adult cells may also carry accumulated mutations [B1]

questions.prompt:
Cloning of goats: 120 pregnancies, 18 live births. Mice: 300 pregnancies, 9 live births.

(i) Calculate the percentage of pregnancies resulting in live births for each. (2)
(ii) Give three factors that should be controlled when comparing data from different laboratories. (3)
questions.solution:
(i) Goats: 15 % [B1]
Mice: 3 % [B1]
(ii) Type / age of donor cell [B1]
Method of nuclear transfer / culture conditions [B1]
Health / age of surrogate mothers / how success was defined [B1]

questions.prompt: Of 277 embryos made by nuclear transfer, 29 were implanted and 1 lamb was born. Calculate the percentage success from embryos and from implantations, and suggest two reasons for the low success. (5)
questions.solution:
From embryos: 0.36 % [B1]
From implantations: 3.4 % [B1]
Donor nucleus not fully reprogrammed / genes not switched on correctly [B1]
Damage to the egg during nuclear transfer [B1]
Embryos fail to implant / abnormalities cause miscarriage [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe uses of cloning in medicine and agriculture. (5)
questions.solution:
Therapeutic cloning — embryonic stem cells genetically matched to a patient [B1]
Producing GM animals that make proteins (pharming) [B1]
Cloning high-yielding farm animals [B1]
Micropropagation of crop plants with desirable traits [B1]
Conserving rare plants / animals [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how to clone a lavender plant by taking a cutting. (4)
questions.solution:
Cut a healthy shoot from the plant, just below a node, with a sharp scalpel [B1]
Remove lower leaves to reduce water loss [B1]
Dip the cut end in rooting powder (auxin) [B1]
Plant in moist compost and cover with a plastic bag / keep humid and warm [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe micropropagation (tissue culture) of plants. (4)
questions.solution:
Small pieces (explants) taken from meristem tissue [B1]
Sterilised and placed on a nutrient medium with plant hormones [B1]
